The stave barns of the Vestmark valley have been repaired board by board by the farmers who work them, for whom a barn is a tool to be kept in working order rather than a record to be consulted. And a conspicuous seam can mislead in its own way: a viewer who sees a sharp break may infer a catastrophe where there was only routine maintenance.

None of this shows that imitative repair is always right. Solvang was correct that a repair makes a claim about the past, and that such claims can be false. But whether a given repair deceives depends on what the building is understood to be, whether document, instrument, or continuing practice, and that question must be answered before the question of seams can be.

passages.title: Calder’s rolling beach easement
passages.text:
Along the coast of the province of Calder, the public has long held a customary right to use the dry-sand beach, the strip between the high-water line and the line of permanent vegetation, even where that strip lies on privately titled land. The right was clear enough so long as the coast stayed put. But Calder’s shore moves. When erosion pushes the vegetation line inland, does the public’s easement move with it, onto ground that was formerly a lawn or a house lot, or does it stay fixed and vanish into the sea?

The Calder High Court answered in Ostrander v. Coastal Lands Board (1979). Borrowing from the older law of river boundaries, the court distinguished erosion, a gradual and imperceptible loss of land, from avulsion, a sudden and perceptible loss such as that caused by a single storm. The easement follows gradual change, so a beach that creeps inland over decades carries the public’s right with it. But when a storm abruptly strips away the dunes, the easement remains where it was, and the newly exposed sand stays private unless natural processes rebuild the beach to its former position. Thus an owner whose dune line retreated thirty meters in one hurricane could fence the exposed sand, whereas a neighbor who lost the same thirty meters over twenty years could not.

Ostrander drew criticism from several directions. Landowners argued that a rolling easement shifted the burden of public use onto land they had never surrendered. Public access advocates raised a more practical objection: if most land loss on Calder’s coast occurs in storms, the avulsion exception would swallow the rule, and within a generation fences would line the shore. Coastal geologists, for their part, doubted that the distinction could be applied at all, since much apparently gradual retreat is the cumulative work of many small storms, while a single storm’s losses are often partly reversed as sand returns in the following months. Judge Imelda Corran, dissenting, wrote that the majority had “imported a distinction made for rivers that move their channels to a shore that moves its sand.”

Later developments lent support to these critics. A provincial survey in 1996 found that in counties with frequent storms, owners had fenced more than a third of the formerly public dry beach, and that much of the fenced sand had in fact partly rebuilt on its own. In Reyes v. Port Allard (2011), the court abandoned the speed-based test. It now asks only whether a shift in the vegetation line has persisted for five years: if it has, the easement moves to the new line however the shift occurred; if the line returns seaward within that period, nothing changes.

The Reyes test has critics of its own, who call the five-year period arbitrary. But it has an evidentiary virtue that Ostrander lacked: it asks courts to determine where a line has stood, not to reconstruct how quickly it got there.

questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs of titles would most likely be found on documents whose relationship to each other is most analogous to the relationship between passage A and passage B?
choices: “In Defense of Open Admission” and “Three Problems with Open Admission”
“Three Problems with Open Admission” and “Three Problems with Selective Admission”
“Three Problems with Open Admission” and “Open Admission at Harlow College: What a Decade of Results Shows”
“The Origins of Open Admission” and “Open Admission at Harlow College: What a Decade of Results Shows”
“Three Problems with Open Admission” and “Why Harlow College Ended Its Experiment with Open Admission”
questions.explanation: Passage A lists numbered problems with participatory budgeting; passage B defends the practice largely through one city’s track record, which matches C’s critique followed by a case-based defense. A is the tempting trap: it has the right two kinds of document but in the reverse order. B makes the second document a critique of a different practice, D mischaracterizes passage A as a history of origins, and E makes the second document a story of failure rather than a defense.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a pair of titles whose relationship matches A-to-B: a list of problems with a practice, then a defense of it built on one place's track record.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The opening sentence of each passage: A's 'raises at least three problems' and B's 'The record of the program's first eight cycles tells a different story.'

breakdown.analysis: Name the relationship before you look at titles. Passage A is a general critique: three numbered problems. Passage B is a rebuttal built on one case, Brennick. So you want: critique of X, then 'here's what happened when one place actually did X, and it went fine.' Order matters here, so check which document is the critique and which is the case study.

choices.note: The two kinds of document are right but the order is flipped: the defense comes first and the critique second. Passage A is the critique. Also, 'In Defense of' is a general defense, not one place's record. This is the trap.
Second title attacks a different practice (selective admission). Passage B defends the same practice A attacks, so this is the wrong relationship.

CORRECT. First title is a numbered critique of a practice, like passage A. Second title looks at one school's decade of results, like passage B's eight cycles in Brennick, which push back on the skeptics. Critique, then a case-based answer.
'The Origins of' makes the first document a history. Passage A mentions Brazil in one clause, but its job is to list problems, not trace origins.
Right first title, wrong second one. 'Why Harlow Ended Its Experiment' is a story of failure, which would back up the critique. Passage B says the program works.

questions.stem: According to passage A, residents choosing among proposed projects tend to favor projects that
choices: produce results residents can readily see
cost the least to complete
benefit their own neighborhoods
have been endorsed by council members
repair or replace existing infrastructure
questions.explanation: The second problem in passage A is that residents ‘predictably favor’ playgrounds, murals, and bike lanes, ‘things they can point to,’ which is A. E reverses the point: passage A says such repairs, like replacing water mains, lose out. C may sound realistic, but passage A never says residents favor their own neighborhoods, and B and D are not mentioned.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Detail question: what kind of projects does passage A say residents favor?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph (the 'Second, the process is biased toward the visible' problem).

breakdown.analysis: This is a pure lookup. Passage A says residents 'predictably favor new playgrounds, murals, and bike lanes—things they can point to' over water mains and road resurfacing. Prephrase: things they can see. Don't add realistic-sounding motives the passage never gives.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Things they can point to' = results they can readily see. Same idea, different words.
Cost never comes up. Nothing says residents pick the cheapest project.
Sounds like real life, and that's why it tempts. But passage A never says residents favor their own neighborhoods. You can't pick an answer on what's plausible; it has to be in the text.
Council endorsements aren't mentioned. If anything, passage A treats council members as the ones dodging responsibility, not steering votes.
Opposite. Replacing water mains and resurfacing roads are the projects that lose out. Repair is what residents pass over.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: participatory budgeting began in Brazil
the times at which participatory budgeting events are held affect who takes part
council members can avoid responsibility for projects that residents chose
allocating funds through participatory budgeting tends to divert money from basic infrastructure such as water systems
taking part in participatory budgeting gives residents a clearer understanding of budgetary trade-offs
questions.explanation: Passage A warns that a city using this process ‘may find its least glamorous infrastructure starved,’ naming water mains; passage B replies that every dollar for water and sewer systems is still allocated by the council, so the program ‘has not crowded out’ ordinary obligations. That is D. B is tempting, but passage B’s account of Brennick’s mail and library voting suggests that it accepts the point that access shapes turnout. A, C, and E are each discussed in only one passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a point where one author would say yes and the other would say no.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph (infrastructure 'starved'); passage B, second paragraph ('Nor has the program crowded out...' and the 98 percent).

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. Passage A worries that letting residents pick projects 'may find its least glamorous infrastructure starved,' naming water mains. Passage B answers directly: the program hasn't crowded out ordinary obligations because every dollar for water and sewer is still set by the council. That's a direct clash. Check every other choice: does each author actually take a side?

choices.note: Only passage A mentions Brazil. Passage B says nothing about origins, so there's no disagreement on record.

Tempting, since passage A raises meeting times. But passage B doesn't deny that timing matters. Brennick's mail and grocery-store voting suggests B agrees that access shapes who participates; it just says Brennick fixed it.
Only passage A discusses accountability. Passage B never addresses it, so we can't say B disagrees.

CORRECT. A says this process tends to starve basic infrastructure like water mains. B says it doesn't, because water and sewer money stays with the council and residents only control 2 percent. Yes vs. no.
Only passage B talks about what participants learn about trade-offs. Passage A is silent, so no disagreement.

questions.stem: The author of passage B mentions the pedestrian crossing near a senior center (middle of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that residents generally rank safety projects above aesthetic ones
support the claim that residents’ choices can address needs that professional planners have missed
illustrate the kind of project the council funds from the remaining 98 percent of the budget
suggest that city engineers are less competent than residents at identifying hazards
give an example of a visible project of the kind that residents tend to prefer
questions.explanation: The crossing is the example (‘for example’) for the claim that residents’ projects ‘have often addressed problems that city engineers had overlooked,’ which is B. D overstates this into a general comparison of competence, and A generalizes one example into a ranking of priorities that passage B never gives. E borrows passage A’s concern with visible projects, but passage B offers the example to show the projects are not frivolous, not to illustrate a taste for the visible.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function question: why does passage B bring up the dangerous crossing near the senior center?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph, the sentence right before the example ('have often addressed problems that city engineers had overlooked').

breakdown.analysis: The words 'for example' tell you the job: the crossing illustrates the claim just before it. That claim is that residents' projects, far from frivolous, often fix problems city engineers missed. The crossing never showed up in a traffic study because no one had died there yet, but residents knew it was dangerous. Prephrase: proof that residents catch needs the professionals overlooked.

choices.note: Too broad. One example doesn't establish a general ranking of safety over aesthetics, and passage B never makes that ranking.
CORRECT. The crossing is the example for 'problems that city engineers had overlooked.' Engineers = professional planners; residents' choices filled the gap.
Wrong pot of money. The crossing was a resident-chosen project from the 2 percent set-aside, not something the council funded from the other 98 percent.
Too strong. Missing one hazard isn't the same as being less competent overall. Passage B says engineers overlooked some problems, not that residents are better at spotting hazards.
Borrows passage A's worry about 'visible' projects. Passage B uses the example to show residents' picks aren't frivolous, which pushes against A's point rather than illustrating it.

questions.stem: The author of passage B suggests that the officials mentioned in the last sentence of passage B are too
choices: generous
deferential
impatient
sentimental
narrow
questions.explanation: Passage B says these officials judge the programs by ‘the wrong yardstick,’ looking only at the size of the sums at stake and ignoring what residents learn. That means their standard of value is too narrow, which is E. ‘Impatient’ (C) may tempt because the officials dismiss the program, but nothing suggests they judged it too soon. The other words have no support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the one word for the flaw passage B sees in the officials who call these programs symbolic.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, last sentence ('measuring them by the wrong yardstick').

breakdown.analysis: The officials judge the programs only by 'the size of the sums at stake' and ignore what residents learn. Their measure looks at one thing and misses another. Prephrase: their standard is too limited. Match that to a single adjective.

choices.note: Opposite direction. 'Generous' would mean they think too highly of the programs. They dismiss them.
'Deferential' means too willing to yield to others. Nothing says the officials defer to anyone; they're dismissing a program.
Tempting because dismissing something can feel hasty. But the complaint is about what they measure, not about when they judged. Nothing suggests they judged too soon.
'Sentimental' means overly emotional. Their mistake is a cold, dollars-only measure, closer to the opposite.
CORRECT. Looking only at the dollar amount and ignoring civic learning is a narrow yardstick. 'Narrow' names exactly that.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage A would be likely to offer regarding the suggestion in passage B that Brennick’s program has not been captured by an unrepresentative group of residents?
choices: Accepting ballots by mail makes it harder to verify that each ballot was cast by an eligible resident.
Figures on who cast ballots reveal little about who took part in deciding which proposals appeared on the ballot.
Even a representative body of voters cannot be held responsible when a project it chose turns out badly.
Eight budget cycles are too few to establish that a pattern of participation will persist.
Residents of low-income neighborhoods are as likely as other residents to favor projects they can point to.
questions.explanation: Passage A’s first problem concerns the proposal meetings, ‘at which residents decide which projects will appear on the ballot,’ which favor residents with free time and confidence. Passage B’s evidence covers only who voted, so passage A would object that turnout figures leave untouched the stage it worries about. That is B. C is the strongest trap: it is passage A’s third problem, but it concedes rather than challenges that the voters were representative. D is a generic objection that passage A gives no basis for, and A and E concern issues passage A never raises about representativeness.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict how passage A's author would attack B's evidence that Brennick's program isn't run by an unrepresentative group.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph (proposal meetings decide what's on the ballot); passage B, first paragraph (ballots by mail, low-income vote share).

breakdown.analysis: Look closely at what each side measures. Passage A's first problem is about the proposal meetings, 'at which residents decide which projects will appear on the ballot,' held on weeknight evenings. Passage B's evidence is about who cast ballots. Those are different stages. It's like saying an election is fair because turnout was high, when the complaint was about who picked the candidates. Prephrase: voter data says nothing about who shaped the ballot.

choices.note: Ballot fraud is a new issue. Passage A never worries about voter eligibility; its complaint is about who participates in shaping choices.

CORRECT. Passage A's worry targets the proposal stage. Passage B only shows who voted. A would say B answered the wrong question: representative voters can still be choosing from a menu set by the unrepresentative few.

This is A's third problem, accountability, so it sounds like A. But it concedes the voters may be representative and moves to another complaint. The question asks for a criticism of B's representativeness claim.
A generic sample-size objection. Passage A gives no reason to think eight cycles is too few, and nothing in A is about time.
Mixes A's second problem (visible projects) with the representativeness issue. Even if true, it doesn't show the participants are unrepresentative.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A raises several objections to a practice; passage B presents evidence that bears against some of those objections and identifies a benefit of the practice that passage A does not discuss.
Passage A raises several objections to a practice; passage B responds in turn to each of those objections, using evidence from a single city.
Passage A traces the origins of a practice; passage B evaluates the results of that practice in one city.
Passage A argues that a practice should be abandoned; passage B argues that the practice should be greatly expanded.
Both passages criticize a practice, but passage B confines its criticism to the version of the practice adopted in one city.
questions.explanation: Passage B answers passage A’s worries about unrepresentative participation and neglected infrastructure, and then adds a benefit passage A never mentions: what participants learn about trade-offs. That is A. B is the trap: passage B never addresses passage A’s third problem, accountability, so it does not respond to ‘each’ objection. C mistakes passage A’s opening mention of Brazil for its purpose, D attributes recommendations neither passage makes, and E misreads passage B as a criticism.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the two passages relate overall.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Both passages as a whole: A's three numbered problems, and B's three paragraphs (turnout, infrastructure, what participants learn).

breakdown.analysis: Map B onto A. A's problem 1 (unrepresentative participants) gets B's paragraph 1 (low-income turnout). A's problem 2 (infrastructure starved) gets B's paragraph 2 (water and sewer stay with council). A's problem 3 (accountability) gets nothing. Then B adds something new: participants learn about trade-offs. So B answers some objections and adds a benefit. Watch for 'each' in the answers.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Some of those objections' is exactly right, since accountability goes unanswered, and the learning benefit is something A never discusses.
Trap. 'Each of those objections' is too much. Passage B never addresses accountability, A's third problem.
Passage A mentions Brazil once in passing. Its job is to raise objections, not to trace origins.
Too strong on both sides. A raises problems but never says to abandon the practice. B defends the practice but never calls for greatly expanding it.
Misreads B. Passage B defends Brennick's program; it isn't a criticism of anything.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: In ground-nesting shorebirds, egg color serves mainly to conceal eggs from predators by matching the color of the nesting site.
Valk’s measurements prove that dark eggs cool more slowly than pale ones in every shorebird species that nests in cold regions.
Kessin sandpiper eggs are darker in the north because the gravel at northern nesting sites is darker than the sand of southern marshes.

The northward darkening of Kessin sandpiper eggs, though it makes them easier for predators to find, is plausibly explained as an adaptation that limits the developmental pauses caused by cooling while the female forages.
Because only the female incubates, the Kessin sandpiper suffers higher rates of nest loss than shorebird species in which both parents share incubation.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the puzzle of northern eggs that are dark despite pale gravel, then sets out Valk’s warming theory with a worked example and supporting evidence. D states that whole arc. A describes only the general pattern in the first paragraph that the sandpiper breaks. B overstates the claim (‘prove,’ ‘every species’), C contradicts the passage’s statement that northern gravel is pale, and E makes a comparison the passage never draws.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Main point: what is the passage as a whole arguing?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage, especially the puzzle at the end of the first paragraph and the last sentence of the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Structure: general rule (eggs match the ground to hide), the sandpiper exception (northern eggs are dark on pale gravel), Valk's explanation (dark eggs stay warm while the female forages), worked numbers, supporting evidence, a caveat. The last sentence sums it up: what looked like bad camouflage is a trade-off between predators and developmental delay. The main point has to include the puzzle and the warmth explanation.

choices.note: Only the background rule from the first paragraph, the thing the sandpiper breaks. It leaves out the whole point.
Way too strong. 'Prove' and 'every shorebird species' go far beyond a study of one species, and the author admits open questions.
Contradicts the passage. The northern gravel is pale; that's what makes the dark eggs a puzzle.

CORRECT. It has the puzzle (darker northward despite being easier to spot) and the explanation (limits the pauses caused by cooling while the female forages). 'Plausibly' matches the author's supportive but not absolute tone.
The passage never compares nest loss with species where both parents incubate. Made-up comparison.

questions.stem: According to the passage, at the southern end of the Kessin sandpiper’s range
choices: dark eggs are found by predators more often than they are in the north
females’ foraging trips are shorter than those of northern females
even pale eggs take more than an hour to cool to the temperature at which embryonic development stops
all of the species’ eggs are pale enough to match the surrounding sand exactly
air temperatures during incubation average about 8°C
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states that in the south, where the air averages near 20°C, ‘even pale eggs took more than an hour to cool to 26°C,’ the threshold at which development stops. That is C. D is tempting because southern eggs are paler, but the passage never says they are uniformly pale or match exactly. E gives the figure for the northern colony, and A and B compare things the passage never measures.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Detail: what does the passage say about the southern end of the range?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last sentence ('At the southern end of the range, by contrast...').

breakdown.analysis: Straight lookup. In the south, air averages near 20°C and 'even pale eggs took more than an hour to cool to 26°C,' so darkening buys nothing. Find the answer that repeats that.

choices.note: The passage never compares how often predators find dark eggs in the south vs. the north. Unsupported comparison.
Foraging trip length is given only for the northern colony (about 25 minutes). No southern figure, so no comparison.
CORRECT. Nearly word for word: pale eggs take more than an hour to reach 26°C, the temperature where development stops.
Tempting since southern eggs are paler. But 'all' and 'exactly' are extreme, and the passage never says southern eggs match the sand perfectly.
Wrong place. 8°C is the northern colony's average. The south is near 20°C.

questions.stem: In using the phrase “pays for itself” (end of the second paragraph), the author most probably means that
choices: producing dark pigment costs the female no more energy than producing pale shells does
dark eggs require the female to spend less total time incubating them
the dark color of the eggs eventually makes them harder for predators to see as the season progresses
the food the female gathers while foraging supplies the materials needed to darken the shells
in cold regions, the protection from developmental delay that dark shells provide outweighs the added risk that they will be detected
questions.explanation: The sentence weighs ‘this benefit,’ slower cooling and therefore fewer developmental pauses, against ‘the eggs’ greater visibility,’ and says the benefit is large enough to justify it. That is E. A reads ‘pays’ as a literal metabolic cost, which the passage never discusses. B may tempt, since fewer pauses shorten incubation, but the phrase concerns weighing a benefit against a predation cost, and the passage says nothing about the female’s time on the nest.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Meaning-in-context: what does 'pays for itself' mean in Valk's claim?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, last sentence ('this benefit is large enough that the darkness pays for itself, despite the eggs' greater visibility').

breakdown.analysis: Read the full sentence. It weighs a benefit (slower cooling, fewer pauses, fewer days in the nest) against a cost (eggs easier for predators to see). 'Pays for itself' means the benefit outweighs the cost, and only 'where breeding-season air is cold.' It's like saying a pricey winter coat pays for itself if you'd otherwise get sick every week. Prephrase: in cold places, the warmth benefit beats the visibility risk.

choices.note: Takes 'pays' literally, as energy cost to make pigment. The passage never discusses pigment cost.
Close but off. Fewer pauses do shorten incubation, but the phrase is about weighing a benefit against a predation cost. Nothing says the female spends less time sitting on the eggs.
Opposite. Dark eggs stay easier to see. The passage never says they become harder to see later in the season.
Invents a link between foraging and shell color. The passage says foraging is why eggs cool, not where pigment comes from.
CORRECT. The benefit is protection from developmental delay, the cost is easier detection, and the claim is limited to cold regions. That's the sentence's trade-off.

questions.stem: The author mentions the two colonies “lying at the same latitude” (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that egg darkness varies with the factor Valk’s theory emphasizes rather than merely with geographic position
suggest that predators are more numerous on islands than in sheltered inland valleys
provide the figures used in the worked example of the third paragraph
identify a case that Valk’s theory has not yet been able to explain
indicate that females at island colonies take longer foraging trips than those inland
questions.explanation: Two colonies at the same latitude but with different temperatures lay eggs of different darkness. This shows that darkness tracks breeding-season temperature, the variable Valk’s theory depends on, rather than position on the map. That is A. D is tempting because the paragraph does mention an open question, but that question concerns pale clutches among northern neighbors, not these two colonies. B and E invent differences the passage never mentions, and C misplaces the example.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function: why does the author bring up two colonies at the same latitude?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, the 'First' observation.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence says darkness 'tracks breeding-season temperature more closely than it tracks latitude.' The two colonies are a controlled comparison: same latitude, different temperature (cold island vs. sheltered valley), and the cold one lays darker eggs. That rules out 'it's just about how far north you are' and points to temperature, which is what Valk's theory depends on.

choices.note: CORRECT. Holding latitude constant and changing temperature shows darkness follows temperature, the variable Valk's warmth theory cares about, not just geographic position.
Predator numbers on islands vs. valleys are never mentioned. Invented difference.
The worked example in the third paragraph uses one northern colony and a southern contrast, with its own figures. The two-colony comparison is a separate piece of evidence.

Tempting because the same paragraph mentions an open question. But that question is about why some northern females lay paler eggs than their neighbors, not about these two colonies, which support the theory.
Foraging trip length at islands vs. inland is never discussed. Invented.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Valk’s theory mentioned in the second paragraph?
choices: At northern colonies, dark eggs are found by predators more often than pale eggs would be at the same sites.
Females at southern colonies take foraging trips that are, on average, somewhat longer than those of northern females.
Several shorebird species that nest alongside the Kessin sandpiper in the north lay pale eggs, and in those species both parents take turns incubating.
Among northern colonies, eggs are no darker at sites where skies are usually clear during the breeding season than at sites that are overcast through most of it.
The pigment that darkens Kessin sandpiper eggs requires the female to use energy that she must replace by foraging.
questions.explanation: The theory’s mechanism is that dark shells ‘absorb more sunlight’ and so cool more slowly; the worked example concerns eggs ‘exposed to sunlight.’ If darkness is equally pronounced where there is little sun to absorb, the trait does not track the benefit the theory says explains it, so D undermines the theory. A is the main trap, but greater visibility is a cost the theory already acknowledges and weighs. C actually fits the theory, since species where both parents incubate seldom leave eggs uncovered. Even longer southern trips (B) would be far shorter than the hour pale eggs take to cool there, and E names a small cost without challenging the trade-off.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Weaken: find the fact that most undercuts Valk's warmth theory.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (the mechanism: dark shells 'absorb more sunlight') and third paragraph (eggs 'exposed to sunlight').

breakdown.analysis: Find the mechanism, then attack it. Valk says dark eggs stay warm because they absorb more sunlight. So if the theory is right, darkness should pay off most where there's sun to absorb. If eggs are just as dark under constant overcast as under clear skies, the trait isn't tracking the benefit that's supposed to explain it. Answers that restate costs the theory already accepts don't hurt it.

choices.note: Trap. Valk already admits dark eggs are easier to spot; that's the cost in the trade-off. Restating a known cost doesn't weaken the claim that the benefit outweighs it.

Northern trips average about 25 minutes, and southern pale eggs take over an hour to cool. 'Somewhat longer' trips in the south still won't reach the threshold, so the theory's prediction for the south holds.
Fits the theory. If both parents take turns, eggs are rarely left uncovered, so there's no cooling problem and no reason to go dark. That's support, not a challenge.

CORRECT. If darkness works by soaking up sunlight, it should help more under clear skies. Equal darkness under heavy overcast means the trait doesn't follow the sunlight benefit, which casts doubt on the theory's explanation.
Adds a small energy cost but says nothing about whether the warmth benefit outweighs the costs. Not enough to challenge the trade-off.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: The darkest Kessin sandpiper eggs are laid at the colonies farthest north in the species’ range.
If females at the northern colony Valk studied typically returned to the nest in less than 15 minutes, dark eggs there would offer little or no developmental advantage over pale ones.
Over a full incubation at the northern colony Valk studied, the embryo in a dark egg would spend no time at all with its development halted.
Kessin sandpiper eggs that are left uncovered in cold air for more than 15 minutes do not hatch.
At the southern end of the range, females spend less time away from the nest each day than females in the north do.
questions.explanation: At the northern colony a pale egg takes about 15 minutes to cool to the 26°C threshold. If trips were shorter than that, pale eggs would never reach the threshold, so dark shells would gain no developmental time, which is B. A is the strongest trap: eggs darken toward the north, but the fourth paragraph says darkness tracks temperature more closely than latitude, so the darkest eggs need not come from the farthest-north colonies. C is too strong, because dark eggs avoid a pause only ‘on most trips.’ D confuses a halt in development with failure to hatch, and E compares something the passage never measures.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Inference: which claim do the passage's facts most strongly support?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (the northern numbers: 15 minutes for a pale egg to cool, 28 for a dark one) and fourth paragraph (temperature vs. latitude).

breakdown.analysis: Use the numbers. At the northern colony, a pale egg hits the 26°C threshold in about 15 minutes. Development only stops after that. So if the female always came back in under 15 minutes, pale eggs would never stall, and dark eggs would have nothing to save. Small worked example: a 10-minute trip leaves pale and dark eggs both above 26°C, zero pause for either.

choices.note: Trap. Eggs darken northward in general, but the fourth paragraph says darkness tracks temperature more than latitude. A colder colony further south could lay darker eggs, so the darkest need not be farthest north.
CORRECT. Pale eggs take about 15 minutes to reach the threshold. Trips shorter than that mean no pause for pale eggs, so dark shells buy no developmental time.
Too strong. Dark eggs avoid a pause 'on most trips,' not all. Some trips are long enough to cause a pause.
Confuses a pause in development with death. The passage says development stops until rewarmed, then resumes. Nothing says those eggs don't hatch.
The passage gives no time-away figures for southern females. Unsupported comparison.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Valk’s theory can best be described as
choices: skepticism about the mechanism on which the theory relies
detached neutrality between the theory and the concealment view it challenges
unreserved enthusiasm for a theory regarded as settling the matter
reluctant acceptance of a theory that conflicts with established findings
favorable regard tempered by acknowledgment that some questions remain unanswered
questions.explanation: The author says that two observations ‘support Valk’s account’ and credits it with turning an apparent lapse into a predictable result. The author also notes that it ‘leaves some questions open,’ which is the mix in E. C ignores that caveat. D is tempting, but the author shows no reluctance, and the theory accepts rather than conflicts with the finding that matched eggs are better concealed. A and B do not fit the author’s explicitly supportive language.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Author's attitude toward Valk's theory.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph: 'Two further observations support Valk's account' and the last sentence ('leaves some questions open... but it turns...').

breakdown.analysis: Find the evaluative words. 'Support Valk's account' and 'turns what looked like a lapse... into the predictable result' are positive. 'Leaves some questions open' is a caveat. So: positive, with a reservation. Attitude answers must match both halves.

choices.note: Opposite. The author lays out the sunlight mechanism with numbers and offers evidence for it; nothing is skeptical about the mechanism.
Not neutral. The author says the evidence supports Valk and praises what the theory explains.
Ignores the caveat. 'Leaves some questions open' rules out 'unreserved' and 'settling the matter.'
No reluctance anywhere. And the theory doesn't conflict with the camouflage findings; it accepts that matched eggs are better hidden and says warmth outweighs that.
CORRECT. Favorable (supports, explains the puzzle) plus tempered (some questions remain). Both halves match.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Solvang’s doctrine should give way to a general policy of imitative repair, which better respects the traditions within which many buildings were made and maintained.
Because new materials weather to match old ones, distinguishable repair cannot be sustained over time, and Solvang’s doctrine therefore defeats itself.
Solvang’s requirement that repairs be visibly distinct rests on an undefended conception of what a building is, and whether a repair deceives cannot be settled until that conception is.
Since few buildings reach us in a single state, conservation architects should abandon the notion of original fabric altogether.
Solvang rightly holds that repairs make claims about the past, but the rebuilding of the Brekke chapel was a poor application of his own doctrine.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph concedes Solvang’s core insight but concludes that whether a repair deceives depends on what the building is understood to be, a question his doctrine skips, which is C. B inflates one complication (the weathering at Brekke, third paragraph) into the thesis. A is too strong, since the author says nothing shows imitative repair is always right, and E misplaces the critique, which targets the doctrine itself rather than one application of it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Main point: what is the author's overall argument about Solvang's doctrine?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage, especially the last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The author describes Solvang's rule (repairs must look different), then pokes holes: what counts as 'old' is unclear, the rule assumes a building is a document and that seams stay visible, and some traditions see faithful copying as continuity. The last paragraph is the thesis: Solvang was right that repairs make claims about the past, but whether a repair deceives depends on what the building is understood to be, and that has to be settled first. The main point is critical but measured.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says 'None of this shows that imitative repair is always right.' Nowhere does the author call for a general policy of imitation.
Takes one complication, the weathering at Brekke, and makes it the whole thesis. It's one problem among several, and the author never says the doctrine defeats itself.

CORRECT. The doctrine rests on an undefended view of what a building is (a document), and the last paragraph says that question must be answered before the seam question can be. That's the conclusion.
Too strong. The author points out that buildings have many layers but never says to drop the idea of original fabric.
Gets the concession right but misplaces the criticism. The author attacks the doctrine itself, not just how Brekke applied it; Brekke is used as the doctrine's own model.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Solvang’s attitude toward imitative repair can best be described as one of
choices: indifference
disapproval
ambivalence
resignation
curiosity
questions.explanation: In the first paragraph Solvang calls imitative repair 'a quiet forgery' that misrepresents one age as another, a clear stance of disapproval (B). Nothing suggests he is torn about it (C) or accepts it as unavoidable (D); his whole doctrine is built to rule it out.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Solvang's attitude toward imitative repair.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, second sentence ('Imitative repair... Solvang regarded as a quiet forgery').

breakdown.analysis: Calling something 'a quiet forgery' is not mild. Solvang thinks imitative repair lies about which age made what, and his whole doctrine exists to replace it. Prephrase: he's against it.

choices.note: He clearly cares. You don't call something a forgery if you're indifferent.
CORRECT. 'Quiet forgery' that presents one age's work as another's is a plain judgment against it.
Ambivalence means mixed feelings. Nothing suggests Solvang sees any good in imitative repair.
Resignation means accepting it as unavoidable. He wants it replaced with distinguishable repair.
Curiosity is neutral interest. His stance is a firm judgment, not an open question.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: recount the history of alterations to the building that the critic used as his principal example
present evidence that the critic’s recommended technique was carelessly executed at the building he admired
introduce the building traditions that are examined in more detail in the fourth paragraph
argue that most visitors to historic buildings take little interest in how those buildings were repaired
identify presuppositions of a view described in the first paragraph and indicate that one of them is not borne out by the critic’s own example
questions.explanation: The third paragraph names two 'undefended assumptions' (the evidentiary relationship and lasting visibility) and shows the second failing at Brekke, Solvang’s own model, which is E. B is the trap: the seam faded through weathering over forty years, not through careless work. A describes the second paragraph, and D overstates the paragraph, which identifies the evidentiary assumption without arguing that visitors are uninterested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function of the third paragraph in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (the 'two undefended assumptions' and the weathered Brekke limestone).

breakdown.analysis: Summarize the paragraph in your own words: the doctrine assumes (1) a building is a document for visitors to read and (2) a visible difference stays visible. Then: at Brekke, Solvang's own model, the cooler limestone weathered to a near match, so assumption 2 failed. Prephrase: names the doctrine's hidden assumptions and shows one fails at the critic's favorite example.

choices.note: That's the second paragraph (the 1720s front and 1860s roof). The third paragraph is about assumptions and weathering.
Trap. The seam faded because limestone weathers over forty years, not because anyone did sloppy work. 'Carelessly executed' isn't supported.
The fourth paragraph's traditions (Ise, Vestmark) aren't introduced in the third paragraph. They come in fresh in the fourth.
Too strong. The paragraph names the 'evidentiary' assumption but never argues that visitors don't care about repairs.
CORRECT. 'Presuppositions' = the two undefended assumptions; 'not borne out by the critic's own example' = the Brekke seam that now needs a guide to find.

questions.stem: The passage raises all of the following as complications for Solvang’s doctrine EXCEPT:
choices: the expense of obtaining replacement materials that differ visibly from a building’s existing fabric
the tendency of contrasting new material to come to resemble the surrounding material over time
the existence of traditions in which faithful reproduction is understood as a form of continuity
the possibility that a conspicuous seam will lead viewers to infer an event that never occurred
the presence in many buildings of alterations made in several different periods
questions.explanation: Cost is never mentioned, so A is the exception. B is the weathering of the Brekke limestone (third paragraph), C is the Ise Shrine and Vestmark barns, D is the seam that suggests catastrophe where there was only maintenance (end of the fourth paragraph), and E is the point about the 1720s front and 1860s roof (second paragraph).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: EXCEPT question: four choices are complications the passage raises for Solvang; find the one it doesn't.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second, third, and fourth paragraphs, where the complications are listed.

breakdown.analysis: Check each choice against the text and cross off the four that appear. The complications in the passage: buildings with many layers of alterations (paragraph 2), assumptions that a building is a document and that seams stay visible (paragraph 3), traditions of faithful reproduction, working barns, and misleading seams (paragraph 4). Whatever's left over is the answer.

choices.note: CORRECT. Money never comes up. The passage never mentions the expense of getting contrasting materials.
In the passage: the cooler Brekke limestone weathered to a near match within forty years (third paragraph).
In the passage: the Ise Grand Shrine, rebuilt in the same form for centuries, treats reproduction as continuity (fourth paragraph).
In the passage: a sharp seam can make viewers infer a catastrophe where there was only routine maintenance (end of fourth paragraph).
In the passage: Brekke's 1720s front and 1860s roof show buildings carry alterations from several periods (second paragraph).

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Solvang’s position commits him to which one of the following views?
choices: The 1720s west front of the Brekke chapel should be treated as new work rather than as original fabric.
Imitative repair is acceptable when a building’s earlier alterations were themselves imitative.
Buildings that are rebuilt at regular intervals in the same form are exempt from the requirement that repairs be distinguishable.
Any future repair to the parts of the Brekke chapel rebuilt in the 1950s should be distinguishable from the 1950s work.
The work done on the Brekke chapel in the 1860s has less historical value than the work done in the 1950s.
questions.explanation: Solvang’s rule is that new work must be distinguishable from the existing fabric it repairs, and the second paragraph notes that the doctrine requires the latest intervention to announce itself. Once the 1950s work is itself old, a new repair to it must be set off from it as well, which is D. A is the trap: it echoes the author’s criticism, but the passage says Solvang in effect treated the 1720s front as though it were original, the opposite of A. C is the author’s complication, not Solvang’s commitment, and E confuses which work must announce itself with which work is more valuable.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Inference: what view does Solvang's position logically commit him to, according to the passage?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph (the rule) and second paragraph ('requires only the latest intervention to announce itself').

breakdown.analysis: Apply the rule forward. Solvang: new work must be distinguishable from the old work it repairs. Today, the 1950s work is part of the existing fabric. So if someone repairs the 1950s parts in the future, that new repair must look different from the 1950s work. Rule → new repair distinguishable from whatever's already there, including the 1950s work.

choices.note: Trap. It echoes the author's complaint, but the passage says Solvang's repairs treated the 1720s front 'as though' it were as original as the medieval nave. He's committed to the opposite of A.
Solvang calls imitative repair forgery. Nothing in his view makes an exception when earlier work was imitative.
That's the author's complication (Ise Shrine), not something Solvang concedes. His doctrine as described has no such exemption.
CORRECT. His rule says the newest work must announce itself against existing fabric. Once the 1950s work is the existing fabric, any later repair to it must be set off from it.
Mixes up which work must stand out with which work is worth more. Making the latest repair visible says nothing about the 1860s roof having less historical value.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to identify which one of the following as the primary reason that Solvang’s doctrine is ill suited to the stave barns of the Vestmark valley?
choices: The timber used in the barns weathers too quickly for any contrast between old and new boards to remain visible.
Those who maintain the barns understand them as tools to be kept in working order rather than as records to be read.
Unlike the Brekke chapel, the barns have no history of alterations made in earlier periods.
Imitative repair is in every case more faithful to a building’s past than distinguishable repair is.
The farmers who repair the barns lack the training needed to produce repairs in a contrasting manner.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the farmers treat a barn as 'a tool to be kept in working order rather than a record to be consulted', and the last paragraph says whether a repair deceives depends on what the building is understood to be, so B. A borrows the weathering problem from the Brekke limestone, which the passage never applies to the barns. C is unsupported (board-by-board repair implies many alterations), and D contradicts the author’s statement that imitative repair is not always right.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Why would the author say Solvang's doctrine doesn't fit the Vestmark barns?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph (the barns sentence) and the last paragraph ('depends on what the building is understood to be').

breakdown.analysis: The passage says the farmers see a barn as 'a tool to be kept in working order rather than a record to be consulted.' Combine that with the thesis: whether a repair deceives depends on whether the building is a document, an instrument, or a practice. Solvang's rule assumes a document. The barns are instruments. Prephrase: the barns aren't records, so the read-the-wounds rule doesn't apply.

choices.note: Borrows the weathering problem from the Brekke limestone. The passage never says the barn timber weathers that way.
CORRECT. The barns are tools, not records. Solvang's doctrine assumes buildings are documents to be read, so it misfits a building understood as a tool.
Unsupported, and likely false. Board-by-board repair over time means many alterations, not none.
Contradicts the author, who says 'None of this shows that imitative repair is always right.' 'In every case' is too strong.
The passage says nothing about the farmers' training or skill. Invented reason.

questions.stem: With which one of the following statements would the author of the passage be most likely to agree?
choices: A repair that is plainly distinguishable from the surrounding fabric can nonetheless convey a misleading impression of a building’s history.
A repair that follows a local tradition of faithful reproduction cannot misrepresent a building’s past.
Conservation architects ought to abandon Solvang’s doctrine in favor of case-by-case judgment.
How a building should be repaired is a more fundamental question than what the building is understood to be.
Visitors to the Brekke chapel today can read its history more easily than visitors could in the 1950s.
questions.explanation: The end of the fourth paragraph says a conspicuous seam 'can mislead in its own way' by suggesting catastrophe where there was only routine maintenance, which supports A. B is the tempting trap, but the author says only that some traditions treat reproduction as continuity and adds that imitative repair is not always right; 'cannot misrepresent' goes beyond that. D reverses the author’s order of questions, and E reverses the weathering point, since the seam now needs a guide.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Which statement would the author most likely agree with?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: End of the fourth paragraph ('a conspicuous seam can mislead in its own way') and the last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The author's last complication is that a sharp seam can make a viewer imagine a catastrophe where there was just routine upkeep. So a clearly visible repair can still mislead. That's a direct match. Watch for answers that turn the author's 'some' and 'can' into 'cannot' or 'ought to abandon.'

choices.note: CORRECT. The author says a conspicuous seam 'can mislead in its own way' by suggesting a catastrophe that didn't happen. Distinguishable, yet misleading.
Too strong. The author says some traditions treat reproduction as continuity, and that a repair can make false claims about the past. 'Cannot misrepresent' goes beyond what the author commits to.
The author questions the doctrine but never prescribes abandoning it or switching to case-by-case judgment. Unsupported recommendation.
Reversed. The author says what the building is understood to be must be answered before the question of seams. That question comes first.
Opposite. The seam has weathered to a near match and now needs a guide to point it out, so today's visitors read the history less easily.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Because a rolling easement shifts title without compensation, the Calder High Court in Reyes sharply limited the circumstances in which the public easement may move.
Later surveys confirmed in every respect Judge Corran’s view that Ostrander had misapplied the law of river boundaries.
Distinctions drawn from the law of river boundaries cannot sensibly be applied to any coastline.

Calder’s rule tying movement of the public beach easement to the speed of shoreline change proved hard to apply and harmful to public access, and it was replaced by a test based on how long a change persists.
Despite the arbitrariness of its five-year period, the Reyes test has resolved each of the controversies that Ostrander provoked.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the problem, through the Ostrander speed-based rule and its criticisms, to the 1996 survey and its replacement by the Reyes persistence test, which D captures. A gives the landowners’ objection, which the passage does not say motivated Reyes. B ('in every respect') and E ('each of the controversies') are too extreme, and E ignores the critics of Reyes in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Main point: what is the passage about overall?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage: the problem (first paragraph), Ostrander (second), criticisms (third), the survey and Reyes (fourth), Reyes' virtue (fifth).

breakdown.analysis: Follow the story. Moving shorelines create a problem. Ostrander answers it with a speed test: gradual erosion moves the easement, sudden storms don't. Critics say that harms public access and can't be applied. The 1996 survey backs them up. Reyes replaces the speed test with a five-year persistence test. The main point has to cover the old rule, why it failed, and its replacement.

choices.note: Gets Reyes backward. Reyes doesn't limit when the easement moves; it moves it after five years 'however the shift occurred.' And the passage never says the landowners' complaint drove Reyes.
'In every respect' is too strong. The survey supported the critics generally; it says nothing about confirming Corran's specific claim about river law in every respect.
Too broad. 'Any coastline' generalizes far beyond Calder, and the passage only discusses this one rule.
CORRECT. Speed-based rule, hard to apply (geologists) and harmful to access (advocates, survey), replaced by a persistence test (Reyes). It covers the full arc.
Too strong. 'Each of the controversies' is extreme, and the last paragraph says Reyes has critics of its own.

questions.stem: The author mentions a neighbor who lost the same thirty meters over twenty years (end of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that gradual erosion is more common on Calder’s coast than storm damage
indicate that the author regards the Ostrander rule as unfair to owners who lose land gradually
illustrate that the Ostrander rule treats equal losses of land differently depending on how rapidly they occurred
show that the Ostrander court misunderstood the law of river boundaries
present a case that the Reyes test would decide differently from the Ostrander rule
questions.explanation: The neighbor is paired with the hurricane-struck owner to show a concrete consequence of the rule: identical thirty-meter losses come out differently depending only on speed, which is C. B is tempting, but the author is describing how the rule works, not passing judgment, at that point. E fails because under Reyes a gradual shift that persists five years also moves the easement, so the neighbor’s case comes out the same.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function: why mention the neighbor who lost thirty meters over twenty years?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, last sentence ('Thus an owner whose dune line retreated thirty meters in one hurricane... whereas a neighbor...').

breakdown.analysis: The sentence starts with 'Thus,' so it shows a consequence of the rule just described. Two owners lose the same thirty meters. One lost it in a storm and can fence it. The other lost it slowly and can't. Same loss, different result, only because of speed. That's the illustration.

choices.note: The passage doesn't say which is more common here. In fact, the advocates later worry that most loss comes from storms.
Tempting, since the contrast might seem unfair. But at this point the author is explaining the rule's results, not judging them, and unfair to which side isn't stated.
CORRECT. Same thirty meters, opposite outcomes, based only on how fast the loss happened. That's exactly what the pair illustrates.
The author describes Ostrander as 'borrowing' from river law without saying here that the court got river law wrong. Corran's critique comes later.
Wrong. Under Reyes, a gradual shift that persists five years moves the easement, so the neighbor's case comes out the same. The hurricane owner's case would differ, not the neighbor's.

questions.stem: The information in the passage most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: Why did the Reyes court choose five years, rather than some other period, as its test of persistence?
How many Calder landowners sought compensation after the Ostrander decision?
Did courts in any other province adopt the rule announced in Ostrander?
What proportion of the sand fenced after Ostrander was eventually returned to public use?
What kind of event did the Ostrander court treat as an avulsion?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph defines avulsion as a sudden and perceptible loss 'such as that caused by a single storm', so E is answerable. A is the trap: the passage mentions critics who call the period arbitrary but never gives the court’s reason. D confuses sand that partly rebuilt naturally (fourth paragraph) with sand returned to public use, and B and C are never addressed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Which question does the passage give enough information to answer?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (the definitions of erosion and avulsion).

breakdown.analysis: For 'which question can be answered' items, test each question against the text. The passage defines avulsion as 'a sudden and perceptible loss such as that caused by a single storm.' That directly answers what event counts as avulsion. The other questions ask for reasons, numbers, or facts the passage doesn't give.

choices.note: Trap. The passage mentions critics calling the five-year period arbitrary, but never gives the court's reason for choosing it.
No count of landowners seeking compensation appears anywhere.
Other provinces' courts are never discussed.
Confuses two things. The survey says much fenced sand partly rebuilt on its own, not that any proportion was returned to public use.
CORRECT. The second paragraph says avulsion is a sudden, perceptible loss, such as one caused by a single storm. Answered.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: Under the Reyes test, the public easement may come to cover sand that was exposed by a single storm.
Under the Ostrander rule, an owner whose vegetation line retreated gradually could fence the newly exposed sand.
The Reyes court adopted its test chiefly in response to landowners’ complaint that the easement shifted onto land they had never surrendered.
Under the Reyes test, the easement moves to a new vegetation line as soon as the line shifts.
Judge Corran maintained that the public easement should remain fixed regardless of how the shoreline changes.
questions.explanation: Reyes moves the easement whenever a shift persists five years 'however the shift occurred', so a storm-exposed strip that stays exposed would come under the easement, which is A. B reverses Ostrander, which let only storm-struck owners fence. D ignores the five-year requirement, and E reads more into Corran’s quoted objection to the river analogy than it says.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Inference: which claim do the passage's facts most strongly support?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph (Reyes: 'however the shift occurred') and second paragraph (Ostrander's rules).

breakdown.analysis: Spell out the Reyes rule: vegetation line shift persists 5+ years → easement moves to the new line, no matter how the shift happened. Line returns seaward within 5 years → nothing changes. So a storm that strips dunes, if the new line holds for five years, moves the easement onto that sand. Under Ostrander that storm-exposed sand would have stayed private.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'However the shift occurred' includes a single storm. If the storm-made line persists five years, the easement covers the exposed sand.
Reversed. Under Ostrander, gradual retreat carries the easement with it, so that owner could not fence. Only storm-struck owners could.
The passage never says the landowners' complaint motivated Reyes. The later developments mentioned support the access and geologist critics.
Ignores the five-year waiting period. The easement moves only once the shift has persisted five years.
Reads too much into Corran's one quoted line. She objected to borrowing a river distinction; she never says the easement should stay fixed no matter what.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the objection to Ostrander raised by public access advocates, as described in the third paragraph?
choices: Many owners of beachfront parcels in Calder bought their land before the public’s customary right was recognized by the courts.
Sand stripped away by a storm is often partly restored by natural processes over the following months.
In the decades after Ostrander, most of the inland retreat of Calder’s vegetation line occurred during brief storms rather than through slow erosion.
The rate of gradual erosion along Calder’s coast increased substantially after 1979.
Courts in several neighboring provinces have declined to recognize any public right to use privately titled beaches.
questions.explanation: The advocates’ objection depends on the conditional premise that most land loss occurs in storms; C confirms it, so the avulsion exception would indeed cover most cases. D points the other way, since more gradual loss means more land over which the easement rolls. B is the geologists’ point and, if anything, suggests some storm losses are temporary, and A bears on the landowners’ objection rather than the advocates’.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Strengthen the public access advocates' objection to Ostrander.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (the advocates' sentence: 'if most land loss on Calder's coast occurs in storms...').

breakdown.analysis: The advocates' argument is conditional: most loss in storms → avulsion exception swallows the rule → fences line the shore. The weak point is the 'if.' Confirm that most land loss happens in storms and the argument goes through. Answers about gradual erosion or about other objections don't help.

choices.note: Relates to the landowners' complaint about land they never surrendered, not the access advocates' worry about fences.
This is the geologists' point. If anything, sand returning suggests some storm losses are temporary, which doesn't support fences lining the shore.
CORRECT. Confirms the advocates' 'if.' If most retreat happens in brief storms, most exposed sand falls under the avulsion exception and stays private.
Points the wrong way. More gradual erosion means more land the easement rolls onto, which helps public access and weakens the worry.
Other provinces are irrelevant to how Ostrander works in Calder.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements about the Reyes test is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: It answers the landowners’ objection that the easement could move onto land they had never surrendered.
It makes irrelevant a factual question that the coastal geologists mentioned in the third paragraph considered difficult to answer.
It moves the easement more promptly than the Ostrander rule did in cases of gradual erosion.
It was adopted by the court on the basis of the findings of the 1996 provincial survey.
It prevents landowners from fencing any portion of the sand exposed by a storm.
questions.explanation: The geologists doubted courts could tell gradual retreat from storm loss; Reyes asks only where the line has stood, 'not ... how quickly it got there' (last paragraph), so that question drops out, which is B. D is the strongest trap: the survey preceded Reyes and 'lent support' to the critics, but the passage never says the court relied on it. A fails because the easement still moves onto private land, and C reverses things, since Reyes waits for five years of persistence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Inference about the Reyes test: what does the passage most strongly support?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (the geologists' doubt) and the last paragraph ('not to reconstruct how quickly it got there').

breakdown.analysis: Connect the geologists to the last paragraph. The geologists doubted anyone could tell gradual erosion from storm loss, since slow retreat is often many small storms. Reyes asks only where the line has stood for five years, not how fast it moved. So the hard question, how quickly did it happen, no longer matters.

choices.note: Fails. Under Reyes the easement still moves onto private land whenever a shift persists, so the landowners' objection stands.
CORRECT. The speed of retreat was the hard question for the geologists. Reyes ignores speed and asks only about persistence, so that question drops out.
Backwards. Under Ostrander the easement followed gradual erosion as it happened. Reyes waits five years, so it's slower, not more prompt.
Strongest trap. The survey came first and 'lent support' to the critics, but the passage never says the Reyes court relied on it. Coming before isn't the same as being the basis.

Too strong. Under Reyes the easement moves only after a shift persists five years, and if the line returns seaward first, nothing changes. The passage never says owners are barred from fencing 'any portion' of storm-exposed sand.

questions.stimulus: Parks director: Last spring, brighter lamps were installed along the walking paths in Fenwick Park. During the following summer, the park had nearly twice as many evening visitors as it had the summer before. Clearly, then, the brighter lamps are what drew the additional visitors to the park after dark.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the parks director's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes that what is true of Fenwick Park must also be true of every other park in the city
relies on visitor counts that may have been gathered by people who favored the new lamps
overlooks the possibility that some other change could account for the increase in evening visitors
takes for granted that the lamps were installed in response to complaints from visitors
fails to establish that the additional visitors stayed in the park longer than earlier visitors did
questions.explanation: The director infers that the lamps caused the rise in evening visitors simply because the rise followed their installation, ignoring other possible causes such as a new event, warmer weather, or new nearby housing; C names this. A is tempting because such arguments often overgeneralize, but this one draws no conclusion about any other park. B, D, and E describe assumptions the argument never makes or needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The brighter lamps are what drew the extra evening visitors to Fenwick Park.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brighter lamps went in last spring; the following summer, evening visitors nearly doubled.

breakdown.analysis: Classic 'it came after, so it caused it' reasoning. The director sees two things happen in sequence and declares one the cause of the other. But lots of things change from one summer to the next: weather, events, new housing nearby, a popular food truck. It's like saying: I started wearing my lucky socks in March and my team won more games in April, so the socks won the games. Prephrase: the argument ignores other possible causes of the jump in visitors.

choices.note: Wrong. This describes an overgeneralization from one park to all parks. The director never says a word about any other park. Tempting only because overgeneralizing is a common flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Brighter lamps boosted visits at Fenwick Park, so brighter lamps will boost visits at every park in the city.

choices.note: Wrong. This is a biased-source attack. Nothing in the stimulus says who counted visitors or that they had a stake in the lamps. You can't pick an answer on a possibility the stimulus never raises.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The lamp company's own staff counted twice as many visitors, so the lamps clearly worked.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the textbook causal flaw. The rise in visitors followed the lamps, but something else (a new event, nicer weather, new apartments nearby) could explain it. The director never rules those out.
Wrong. Why the lamps were installed doesn't matter to whether they caused more visits. The argument makes no assumption about complaints.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The city installed lamps, so residents must have been complaining about the dark.

choices.note: Wrong. The conclusion is about drawing more visitors, not about how long they stayed. The argument doesn't need visit length at all. The LSAT is ultra specific: this is about the number of visitors.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The lamps made the park more enjoyable, since more people came, so people must be staying longer.

questions.stimulus: Theater critic: The Harrow Playhouse should not abandon its practice of staging one new play by a local writer each season. Admittedly, these productions sell fewer tickets than the playhouse's revivals of familiar classics. But several plays that premiered at the Harrow have gone on to successful runs elsewhere, and that reputation for discovery is a major reason donors continue to support the playhouse.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: The Harrow Playhouse should continue staging one new play by a local writer each season.
The Harrow's productions of new local plays sell fewer tickets than its revivals of classics.
Several plays that premiered at the Harrow Playhouse have gone on to successful runs elsewhere.
Donors support the Harrow Playhouse mainly because of its reputation for discovering new plays.
The Harrow Playhouse should stage more new plays and fewer revivals of familiar classics.
questions.explanation: The first sentence is the conclusion: the playhouse should keep its practice of one new local play per season, and the rest of the stimulus concedes a cost and then gives reasons for keeping it, so A is correct. D distorts a premise (the critic says the reputation is 'a major reason,' not the main one), B is the conceded point, and E goes further than the critic, who argues only for keeping the current practice.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Harrow Playhouse should not abandon staging one new local play each season.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Concession: new plays sell fewer tickets than revivals; but several Harrow premieres succeeded elsewhere; that reputation for discovery is a major reason donors keep giving.

breakdown.analysis: The structure is conclusion first, then 'Admittedly...' (a concession), then 'But...' (the reasons). The concession and the reasons all serve the opening sentence. Quick test: ask 'why?' after each sentence. Why shouldn't they abandon it? Because of the reputation and the donors. That tells you the first sentence is the point. Prephrase: keep doing the one-new-local-play-a-year thing.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Should not abandon' the practice is the same as 'should continue' it. This is just the first sentence, restated.
Wrong. This is the concession, introduced by 'Admittedly.' The critic grants it and then argues past it. A conceded point is never the conclusion.
Wrong. This is a premise. It's offered as support for why the practice is worth keeping.

Wrong. It distorts a premise. The critic says the reputation is 'a major reason' donors give, not the main reason. Watch the switch from 'a major' to 'mainly.' And even accurately stated, it's support, not the conclusion.
Wrong. Too strong. The critic only argues for keeping the current practice of one new play per season, not for adding more new plays or cutting revivals.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologists studying marsh wrens in the Teller Wetlands found that each male builds several dummy nests in addition to the nest in which eggs are laid. Building these extra nests costs the birds considerable time and energy. Yet wrens that build more dummy nests tend to raise more chicks than wrens that build fewer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how building dummy nests could increase the number of chicks a wren raises?
choices: Female wrens typically lay the same number of eggs regardless of how many nests the male has built.
Dummy nests are usually built from the same materials as the nests that hold eggs.
Wrens in the Teller Wetlands build more dummy nests in years when the insects they feed their chicks are plentiful.
Some other bird species in the Teller Wetlands also build nests that they never use.
Predators that find an empty dummy nest often stop searching the area before finding the nest with eggs.
questions.explanation: The stem asks how building dummy nests could itself lead to more chicks. E supplies a mechanism: dummy nests divert predators, so more eggs and chicks survive. C is the attractive trap, but it offers a different cause (plentiful food), suggesting the link is not causal, rather than explaining how the nests help; A, if anything, rules out one possible mechanism.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Building dummy nests costs male wrens a lot of time and energy, but wrens that build more dummy nests raise more chicks.

breakdown.analysis: The stem is specific: explain HOW building dummy nests could increase the number of chicks. So you need a mechanism where the dummy nests themselves help chicks survive or get produced. Prephrase: the dummy nests protect the real nest somehow (decoys), or they attract more mates. Think of a shell game: put the prize under one of five cups and a thief has worse odds than if there's only one cup.

choices.note: Wrong. If anything, this rules out one possible mechanism (more nests → more eggs). It doesn't explain how the nests lead to more chicks.
Wrong. Irrelevant. What the nests are made of says nothing about why more of them means more chicks.

Wrong. This is the trap. It offers a different cause, plentiful food, that drives both nest-building and chick-raising. That suggests the nests don't cause anything. The stem asks how the nests themselves could help, so an alternative cause doesn't answer it.
Wrong. Other species doing something similar doesn't explain how it helps wrens raise chicks. Out of scope.

CORRECT. This is the mechanism. Predators find an empty decoy, give up, and the real nest survives. More dummy nests means more decoys, so more eggs make it and more chicks get raised. The cost is worth it.

questions.stimulus: Nutritionist: In a survey of office workers, those who ate breakfast every day reported feeling more alert during morning meetings than did those who usually skipped breakfast. Hence, eating breakfast increases a person's alertness in the morning.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the nutritionist's argument?
choices: Many of the office workers surveyed drank coffee during their morning meetings.
Most of the surveyed workers who usually skipped breakfast also reported getting far less sleep than the breakfast eaters.
Some foods commonly eaten at breakfast contain more sugar than nutritionists recommend.
A few of the surveyed workers who ate breakfast every day reported feeling tired and distracted during their afternoon meetings at work.
Office workers who usually skip breakfast tend to eat a noticeably larger lunch than office workers who eat breakfast.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from a correlation to the claim that breakfast causes alertness. B offers an alternative cause: the breakfast skippers also sleep much less, which could explain their lower alertness. A would matter only if coffee drinking differed between the two groups, which it does not say; D concerns afternoons, and E concerns lunch.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eating breakfast increases a person's morning alertness.

setup.label: Reasoning
