setup.text: In a survey, office workers who ate breakfast daily reported feeling more alert in morning meetings than those who usually skipped it.

breakdown.analysis: Correlation to causation. Breakfast eaters feel more alert, so breakfast causes alertness. To weaken, find something else that differs between the two groups and could explain the alertness gap. Prephrase: the breakfast eaters differ in some other way, like sleep or overall health habits. It's like saying people who own running shoes are fitter, so buying running shoes makes you fit.

choices.note: Wrong. Coffee would matter only if one group drank more of it than the other. 'Many' of all workers drank coffee tells you nothing about a difference between the groups.
CORRECT. Alternative cause. The breakfast skippers also slept far less. Lack of sleep could easily explain why they felt less alert, with breakfast doing nothing at all.
Wrong. Sugar content and nutritionists' recommendations have nothing to do with whether breakfast affects alertness.
Wrong. The conclusion is about morning alertness. 'A few' breakfast eaters feeling tired in the afternoon is the wrong time of day and too small a group to matter.
Wrong. Lunch size doesn't bear on morning alertness, since lunch comes after the morning meetings.

questions.stimulus:
Ruiz: The Brookfield Public Library's main branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays. Many residents work until 6 p.m. or later, and the current 7 p.m. closing time leaves them almost no chance to use the library during the week.

Okafor: The library's budget is fixed, so longer hours would mean buying fewer new books. Residents who work late can still visit on Saturdays, and most of what the library offers is available online at any hour.
questions.stem: Ruiz and Okafor disagree over whether
choices: many Brookfield residents work until 6 p.m. or later
most of the library's offerings can be used online at any hour
residents who work late are able to visit the library on Saturdays
the library's main branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays
the library's budget should be increased to pay for keeping the main branch open longer
questions.explanation: Ruiz proposes the later weekday closing, and Okafor gives reasons against adopting it (fewer books, and other ways to use the library), so they disagree about D. Okafor never disputes that many residents work late (A), and Ruiz says nothing about online offerings (B) or Saturday visits (C); C is tempting because Okafor raises it, but Ruiz's complaint is specifically about weekdays. Neither proposes a larger budget (E).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ruiz: The main branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays because many residents work until 6 or later and can't get there before 7; Okafor: Longer hours would cost new books, late workers can come Saturdays, and most offerings are online.

breakdown.analysis: Okafor never says 'no' in so many words, but every point is a reason against the later hours. Ruiz proposes; Okafor rebuts. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. On the 10 p.m. weekday closing, Ruiz says yes and Okafor clearly says no. Prephrase: whether the library should stay open later on weekdays.

choices.note: Wrong. Ruiz says it, but Okafor never disputes it. In fact Okafor talks about 'residents who work late' as if they exist. No disagreement.
Wrong. Only Okafor talks about online offerings. Ruiz has no stated view, so you can't say they disagree.

Wrong. Tempting because Okafor raises Saturdays as a response. But Ruiz's complaint is specifically about weekdays and never says late workers can't come on Saturday. Ruiz has no stated position here.
CORRECT. Ruiz explicitly says the branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays. Okafor's whole response is a set of reasons not to do it. Yes versus no.
Wrong. Neither speaker proposes raising the budget. Okafor treats the budget as fixed, and Ruiz never mentions it.

questions.stimulus: At Linden Middle School's library, a student may borrow a laptop overnight only if the student has a signed permission form on file. Every student who has a signed permission form on file has also completed the library's device-care session. Rosa borrowed a laptop overnight last Tuesday.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Rosa has completed the library's device-care session.
Any student who has completed the device-care session may borrow a laptop overnight.
Rosa has borrowed a laptop overnight on more than one occasion.
Some students who have signed permission forms on file have never borrowed a laptop overnight.
Students without signed permission forms on file cannot borrow anything from the library.
questions.explanation: Rosa borrowed a laptop overnight, so she must have a signed form on file, and everyone with a signed form has completed the device-care session; hence A. B reverses the conditions: the session and the form are required for borrowing, not enough for it. E overextends a rule about laptops to all library items, and C and D are possible but not guaranteed.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Borrow a laptop overnight → signed permission form on file; 2) Signed form → completed device-care session; 3) Rosa borrowed a laptop overnight last Tuesday.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: Borrowed overnight → signed form → device-care session. Rosa borrowed overnight, so she has a form, so she completed the session. Contrapositive: no session → no form → can't borrow overnight. Remember 'only if' introduces the necessary condition: borrowing only if form means borrow → form, not the reverse.

choices.note: CORRECT. Follow the chain: Rosa borrowed overnight → she has a signed form → she completed the device-care session. Guaranteed.

Wrong. This reverses the logic. The session (and the form) are requirements for borrowing, not tickets that guarantee it. Like saying anyone with a driver's license may drive any car. Having the requirement isn't enough.
Wrong. We know about one borrowing, last Tuesday. Whether she ever borrowed before is unknown. Possible, but not guaranteed.
Wrong. Possible, but nothing forces it. Every student with a form might have borrowed a laptop at some point.
Wrong. Overextends. The rule is only about borrowing laptops overnight. It says nothing about books or anything else the library lends.

questions.stimulus: Geologist: A layer of volcanic ash in the cliffs above Maren Bay matches, in chemical composition, the ash produced by an eruption of Mount Askel about 9,000 years ago. Therefore, the sediment layers lying directly beneath this ash in the cliffs were deposited more than about 9,000 years ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the geologist's argument?
choices: The eruption of Mount Askel was the largest eruption in the region in the last 9,000 years.
Ash from the Mount Askel eruption can be found at many sites besides Maren Bay.
No eruption much more recent than 9,000 years ago produced ash chemically identical to the Askel ash.
The sediment layers beneath the ash at Maren Bay were deposited at a steady rate.
Volcanic ash is the most reliable means geologists have for dating sediment layers.
questions.explanation: The argument dates the ash layer by its chemical match to the Askel eruption, so it requires that the match not have some other, later source. Negate C: if a much later eruption produced identical ash, the layer could be far younger, and the dating collapses. A is the tempting trap because size seems to matter, but the eruption need not be the largest for the match to identify it; B, D, and E are not needed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The sediment layers directly beneath the ash in the Maren Bay cliffs were deposited more than about 9,000 years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The ash layer matches, chemically, the ash from Mount Askel's eruption about 9,000 years ago; layers below are older than layers above.

breakdown.analysis: The geologist dates the ash by matching it to Askel's eruption. That only works if the match actually pins the ash to that eruption. If some other, later eruption could produce the same chemical fingerprint, the ash could be much younger and so could the layers under it. It's like identifying someone by a fingerprint: you're assuming nobody else has the same print. Prephrase: no other, later source produced matching ash.

choices.note: Wrong. Not needed. The eruption doesn't have to be the biggest for its ash to be identified by chemistry. Negating it doesn't hurt the argument. Tempting because size feels like it should matter.
choices.negation: The Mount Askel eruption was not the largest eruption in the region in the last 9,000 years.

choices.note: Wrong. Whether Askel ash shows up elsewhere doesn't affect dating the layer at Maren Bay. Negating it does no harm.
choices.negation: Ash from the Mount Askel eruption cannot be found at many sites besides Maren Bay.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it and the argument falls apart: if a much more recent eruption produced chemically identical ash, then the ash at Maren Bay might come from that eruption, and the layers beneath could be much younger than 9,000 years.
choices.negation: Some eruption much more recent than 9,000 years ago produced ash chemically identical to the Askel ash.

choices.note: Wrong. Deposit rate would matter if you were calculating how old a layer is from its thickness. The argument only claims the layers under the ash are older than the ash. Uneven deposition doesn't change that. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: The sediment layers beneath the ash were not deposited at a steady rate.

choices.note: Wrong. Too strong. The method just has to work here, not be the most reliable method there is. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Volcanic ash is not the most reliable means geologists have for dating sediment layers.

questions.stimulus: Utility spokesperson: Last year Coralton Electric began sending some of its customers monthly reports comparing their electricity use with that of similar nearby households. Over the following year, customers who received the reports used 4 percent less electricity than they had the year before. So the reports led those customers to reduce their electricity use.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the spokesperson's argument?
choices: Electricity prices in Coralton's service area rose noticeably during the year in which the reports were first being sent out.
Many of the customers who received the reports said they found them confusing.
On average, customers who received the reports used more electricity than the similar households they were compared with.
Several other utilities have begun sending similar reports to their customers.
Customers randomly chosen not to receive the reports used about as much electricity as they had the year before.
questions.explanation: The argument attributes a drop in use to the reports, so it is vulnerable to other causes that would have reduced everyone's use. E supplies a control group: comparable customers without reports did not cut back, which makes the reports the likely cause. A is a trap that actually weakens by offering an alternative cause (higher prices), and C and D do not bear on whether the reports caused the drop.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The comparison reports led customers to cut their electricity use.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Customers who got the reports used 4 percent less electricity than the year before.

breakdown.analysis: Another causal argument with no comparison. Maybe everyone used less last year, thanks to mild weather, price hikes, or new appliances. To strengthen, rule out those alternatives. Best tool: a control group. If similar customers who didn't get reports didn't cut back, the reports look like the cause. Prephrase: customers without reports didn't reduce their use.

choices.note: Wrong. This is a trap that weakens. Higher prices are an alternative reason customers would use less electricity, reports or not.
Wrong. If anything, confusing reports make it less likely they changed behavior. Doesn't strengthen.
Wrong. Knowing they started out above their neighbors might suggest a motive to cut back, but it doesn't show the reports actually caused the drop. Other causes are still on the table.
Wrong. What other utilities are doing tells you nothing about whether Coralton's reports worked.

CORRECT. A random control group. Customers randomly kept from getting reports used about the same as before, so whatever changed last year wasn't pushing everyone down. That points to the reports as the cause of the 4 percent drop.

questions.stimulus: After Dunmore County raised its minimum wage last year, employment at the county's restaurants did not decline. However, the average number of hours worked per restaurant employee fell by about 10 percent, and restaurants posted fewer job openings than in previous years. Over the same period, the rate at which restaurant employees quit their jobs dropped sharply.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The increase in the minimum wage is what caused the county's restaurants to reduce the hours their employees worked.
Fewer employees leaving their jobs may account for part of the decline in the restaurants' job openings.
Restaurant employees in Dunmore County earned less in total last year than they had the year before.
The number of people employed at the county's restaurants rose after the minimum wage was increased.
Restaurants that reduced their employees' hours posted fewer job openings than other restaurants did.
questions.explanation: Job openings arise largely when workers leave, so a sharp drop in quitting gives a plausible partial explanation for fewer openings; B's hedged claim is well supported. A is the tempting trap, but the facts show only that hours fell after the wage rose, not that the wage increase caused it. C cannot be determined without knowing how much hourly pay rose, D goes beyond 'did not decline,' and E compares restaurants the facts never distinguish.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) After the minimum wage rose, restaurant employment did not decline; 2) Average hours per employee fell about 10 percent; 3) Restaurants posted fewer job openings than in previous years; 4) The rate at which restaurant employees quit dropped sharply.

breakdown.analysis: No conclusion here, so look for the answer the facts back up without stretching. Think about where job openings come from: mostly from people leaving. If far fewer people quit, there are fewer spots to fill, so fewer openings. That's a solid, hedged inference. Be suspicious of anything claiming causation from the wage increase; the facts only give timing.

choices.note: Wrong. Tempting, but it's causal. The facts say hours fell after the wage rose, not because of it. Something else could have cut hours. Timing isn't proof.
CORRECT. The hedge ('may account for part of') makes this easy to support. Fewer people quitting means fewer vacancies to fill, which plausibly explains some of the drop in openings.
Wrong. Hours fell 10 percent, but hourly pay rose by an unknown amount. If the wage went up 20 percent, total pay could still rise. Can't be determined.
Wrong. 'Did not decline' means stayed the same or rose. You can't conclude it rose. Watch that shift.
Wrong. The facts give county-wide averages and never break restaurants into groups. This comparison has no support.

questions.stimulus: Council member Ibsen argues that the city should close the dog run in Larkspur Park because too few residents use it to justify what it costs to maintain. Yet Ibsen's own figures show that more residents use the dog run each week than use the park's tennis courts, which cost even more to maintain, and Ibsen has argued for keeping the tennis courts. So Ibsen's argument for closing the dog run should be rejected.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by
choices: questioning the accuracy of the figures on which Ibsen bases a proposal
arguing that a facility should be kept because it is more popular than any other facility in the park
criticizing Ibsen's motives rather than the substance of Ibsen's proposal
showing that the reasoning behind Ibsen's proposal, if applied consistently, would support a conclusion that Ibsen rejects
proposing a different way to reduce the cost of maintaining the park's facilities
questions.explanation: The arguer accepts Ibsen's figures and points out that Ibsen's standard (low use relative to cost justifies closing) would condemn the tennis courts even more, yet Ibsen wants to keep them; that is D. B is tempting, but the argument compares the dog run only with the tennis courts and does not claim it is the most popular facility. A is wrong because the argument relies on Ibsen's figures rather than disputing them.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ibsen's argument for closing the dog run should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ibsen says the dog run should close because too few use it to justify its cost; Ibsen's own figures show more people use the dog run than the tennis courts, which cost even more; Ibsen wants to keep the tennis courts.

breakdown.analysis: The arguer takes Ibsen's own standard (low use relative to cost → close it) and applies it to the tennis courts. By that standard, the courts are worse, yet Ibsen wants to keep them. So Ibsen's reasoning is inconsistent. It's like a friend who says you should quit the gym because you only go twice a week, while they keep their own membership and go once a week. Prephrase: shows Ibsen's principle, applied consistently, leads somewhere Ibsen rejects.

choices.note: Wrong. The arguer uses Ibsen's figures, not questions them. The whole point depends on those numbers being right.
choices.example: Example of method: Ibsen says only 20 people a week use the dog run, but that count was taken during a rainy month, so it understates use.

choices.note: Wrong. Tempting because the dog run beats the tennis courts. But the argument compares it to just one facility, never claims it's the most popular in the park, and doesn't even conclude it should be kept, only that Ibsen's argument fails.
choices.example: Example of method: The dog run draws more visitors than the courts, the pool, or the playground, so it should stay open.

choices.note: Wrong. The argument doesn't touch Ibsen's motives. It attacks the consistency of Ibsen's reasoning.
choices.example: Example of method: Ibsen only wants the dog run closed because Ibsen dislikes dogs, so the proposal should be ignored.

choices.note: CORRECT. That's exactly what happens. Ibsen's standard, applied to the tennis courts, would mean closing them too, and Ibsen rejects that conclusion. So the reasoning is inconsistent.
Wrong. No alternative cost-saving plan appears. The arguer only rejects Ibsen's argument.
choices.example: Example of method: Instead of closing the dog run, the city could have volunteers maintain it and save the same money.

questions.stimulus: Energy analyst: Ten years ago, rooftop solar panels generated 5 percent of the electricity used by households in Velmont. Today they generate 9 percent. So Velmont households now use less electricity from sources other than rooftop solar than they did ten years ago.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the energy analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that a trend observed over the past decade will continue at the same pace into the next
ignores that a smaller percentage of a larger total can exceed a larger percentage of a smaller one
assumes without justification that rooftop solar panels are less costly than other sources of electricity
treats evidence about electricity used by households as though it applied to businesses as well
fails to consider whether households in other towns have experienced a similar trend
questions.explanation: The non-solar share fell from 95 to 91 percent, but if total household use rose by more than about 4.4 percent, the amount drawn from non-solar sources actually increased; B describes this percent-versus-amount error. A is tempting, but the conclusion is about the present, not a prediction. D describes a confusion the argument never makes, since it concerns only households, and C and E raise matters the conclusion does not depend on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Velmont households now use less electricity from non-solar sources than ten years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Rooftop solar's share of household electricity rose from 5 percent to 9 percent.

breakdown.analysis: The analyst goes from percentages to amounts. Non-solar's share dropped from 95 to 91 percent, but a smaller slice of a bigger pie can be more pie. Worked example: ten years ago households used 100 units, 95 non-solar. Today they use 120 units; 91 percent of 120 is about 109 non-solar units. That's more, not less. Prephrase: the argument ignores that total use may have grown.

choices.note: Wrong. The conclusion is about now versus ten years ago, not a prediction about the next decade. Tempting because 'trend' sounds right, but there's no forecast here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Solar's share grew 4 points over the last decade, so it will be at 13 percent ten years from now.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the percent-versus-amount error. If total household use grew by more than about 4.4 percent, 91 percent of the new total exceeds 95 percent of the old one, so non-solar use actually went up.
Wrong. Cost never comes up. The conclusion is about how much non-solar electricity is used, and the argument doesn't depend on solar being cheaper.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Households are switching to solar, so solar must be the cheaper option.

choices.note: Wrong. The argument talks only about households, start to finish. It never extends anything to businesses.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Households now get 9 percent of their power from solar, so Velmont businesses must too.

choices.note: Wrong. Other towns are irrelevant. The conclusion is only about Velmont, and what happened elsewhere wouldn't fix or reveal the percent problem.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Velmont's solar share rose, so the national trend must be toward solar too.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Gray shrikes in the Ostrava Hills impale the insects they catch on thorns before eating them. One grasshopper species common in the hills carries a toxin that breaks down within two days after the insect dies. Shrikes eat most impaled prey within a few hours, but they leave impaled grasshoppers of this species on the thorns for two days or more before eating them. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the ecologist's argument?
choices: shrikes impale prey on thorns chiefly in order to make toxic prey safe to eat
the toxin carried by these grasshoppers is harmful to most bird species
shrikes would eat more of these grasshoppers if their toxin broke down more quickly
shrikes in the Ostrava Hills catch more grasshoppers than any other kind of prey
the shrikes' practice of impaling prey may help protect them from the grasshoppers' toxin
questions.explanation: Shrikes wait just long enough for the toxin to break down before eating these grasshoppers, so impaling, which lets them store the prey, plausibly protects them from the toxin, as E cautiously states. A overreaches with 'chiefly': shrikes impale all their prey, most of which they eat within hours, so detoxifying cannot be the main purpose. B, C, and D go beyond anything the facts establish.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Shrikes impale insects they catch on thorns before eating them; 2) One common grasshopper carries a toxin that breaks down within two days after it dies; 3) Shrikes eat most impaled prey within hours; 4) They leave these grasshoppers impaled for two days or more before eating them.

breakdown.analysis: The facts line up suspiciously well: the toxin breaks down in two days, and shrikes wait two days or more before eating these grasshoppers. So impaling gives them a way to store the toxic prey until it's safe. That's the inference. But careful: shrikes impale everything, and eat most prey within hours, so detox can't be the main reason they impale. Prephrase: impaling may help shrikes avoid the toxin.

choices.note: Wrong. Too strong with 'chiefly.' Shrikes impale all their prey and eat most of it within a few hours, so detoxifying can't be the main purpose. It's one benefit for one species of prey.
Wrong. The facts are only about shrikes and this grasshopper. Nothing tells you about most bird species.
Wrong. Unsupported prediction. Nothing says shrikes are limited by the wait. They might eat exactly as many either way.
Wrong. Nothing about how much of their diet is grasshoppers. 'Common in the hills' isn't 'most-caught prey.'

CORRECT. The hedge ('may help') makes it easy to support. The waiting time matches the toxin's breakdown time, and impaling is what lets them store prey that long. So impaling plausibly protects them from the toxin.

questions.stimulus: Principal: Any course that requires students to complete a substantial independent research project develops students' ability to evaluate sources. Every course in Fairview High School's new humanities sequence requires such a project. Therefore, every course in the new humanities sequence should count toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the principal's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any course that develops students' ability to evaluate sources should count toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
Only courses that develop students' ability to evaluate sources should count toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
Students who complete independent research projects evaluate sources better than students who do not.
Every course that counts toward the information-literacy requirement requires a substantial independent research project.
Most courses outside the new humanities sequence do not develop students' ability to evaluate sources.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that every course in the sequence develops students' ability to evaluate sources; A links that property to counting toward the requirement, so the conclusion follows. B is the attractive trap but reverses the needed conditional: it makes source evaluation necessary for counting, not sufficient. D likewise reverses direction, and C and E do not connect the courses to the requirement.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Every course in the new humanities sequence should count toward the information-literacy requirement.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Substantial research project → develops source evaluation; every course in the sequence requires such a project.

breakdown.analysis: Map the chain. Humanities sequence course → research project → develops source evaluation. The conclusion jumps to → should count toward info-literacy. The missing link: develops source evaluation → should count. Full chain: sequence course → research project → source evaluation → counts. Like: all my roommates are nurses, all nurses work nights, so my roommates should get the night-shift discount. You need 'night workers get the discount.'

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the missing link: develops source evaluation → should count. Plug it in and the chain is complete: sequence course → project → source evaluation → counts.

Wrong. This is the trap. 'Only' flips it: counts → develops source evaluation. That makes source evaluation necessary for counting, not enough to guarantee it. The courses could meet it and still not count.
Wrong. A comparison between students doesn't link anything to the requirement. The conclusion's new term, counting toward info-literacy, never shows up.
Wrong. Reversed direction: counts → research project. We need research project (or source evaluation) → counts. Knowing what counting requires doesn't tell you these courses qualify.
Wrong. Courses outside the sequence are irrelevant, and this never connects to the requirement.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: The Dalby Cannery cut its workers' hourly wages last month, citing recent losses. But two years ago, when the workers agreed to forgo a scheduled raise, the owners promised that wages would not be reduced so long as the cannery remained profitable over each full year. The cannery made a profit last year despite its losses in recent months. So the wage cut was unjustified.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, would most help to justify the columnist's argument?
choices: An employer that asks its workers to forgo a scheduled raise should fully explain the financial reasons behind the request.
Wage reductions are justified only when they are genuinely needed to keep a company from going out of business.
Workers who make a concession in exchange for an employer's promise are owed that promise whenever its stated conditions are met.
A company's owners may reduce wages whenever the company's monthly costs exceed its monthly revenue, regardless of its annual results.
Promises that employers make during labor negotiations are binding only if they have been put in writing.
questions.explanation: The columnist's case rests on the promise: workers gave up a raise, the promised condition (a profitable full year) held, so cutting wages broke the promise; C states exactly that principle. B is tempting, but nothing in the argument says the cut was not needed to keep the cannery open, so B could not establish the conclusion. D supports the cannery, and E would undercut the columnist unless the promise was written, which is not stated.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The cannery's wage cut was unjustified.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Two years ago workers gave up a scheduled raise; the owners promised no wage cuts as long as the cannery stayed profitable over each full year; the cannery was profitable last year.

breakdown.analysis: The argument is all about a deal: workers gave something up, the owners promised something back, and the promise's condition was met. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. Here: if workers made a concession for a promise and the promise's conditions are met, the employer must keep it. That makes the cut unjustified. Prephrase: a promise made in exchange for a concession must be kept when its conditions hold.

choices.note: Wrong. About explaining reasons for asking workers to forgo a raise. That's not the issue. The question is whether cutting wages later was justified.
Wrong. Tempting, because it limits wage cuts. But the argument never says the cut wasn't needed to keep the cannery alive. Without that fact, B can't get you to 'unjustified.'

CORRECT. Workers made a concession (forgoing the raise) in exchange for a promise (no cuts while profitable for the full year), and the condition was met (profit last year). So they were owed the promise, and the cut was unjustified.
Wrong. Opposite. This would justify the cut, since recent months showed losses, regardless of the annual profit.
Wrong. This would hurt the columnist unless the promise was written down, which the stimulus never says. It doesn't help reach the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Every film shown at the Corvo Festival this year was chosen by the festival's selection jury, and the jury chose no film that had already been released commercially. The Long Field has already been released commercially, so it was not shown at the Corvo Festival this year.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every car sold at Henley Motors is inspected by Pratt, and Pratt inspects no car that has more than 100,000 miles on it. So the sedan Pratt inspected last week has fewer than 100,000 miles on it.
Every member of the choir auditioned for the director, and the director turned away no one who could read music. Since Lin can read music, Lin is a member of the choir.
All of the paintings in the east gallery were donated by Ames, and Ames donated no painting made before 1900. The Tolland portrait was made before 1900, so Ames did not donate it.
Every dish on the Corbel Café's lunch menu is prepared by its head chef, and the head chef prepares no dish that contains peanuts. The café's satay contains peanuts, so it is not on the lunch menu.
Every book in the reading room was approved by the librarian, and the librarian approves only books in good condition. This atlas is in good condition, so it must be in the reading room.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two rules (shown at the festival → chosen by the jury; chosen by the jury → not released commercially) and, from an item lacking the final property, concludes by contrapositive that it lacks the first: it was not shown. D matches step for step: the satay contains peanuts, so the chef did not prepare it, so it is not on the menu. C is the most tempting trap, but it concludes only that the painting was not donated by Ames, never using the gallery premise to reach a conclusion about the gallery; A runs forward from the middle term, and B and E reverse the conditionals.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Long Field was not shown at the Corvo Festival this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Shown at festival → chosen by the jury; chosen by the jury → not released commercially; The Long Field was released commercially.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; no B is C; this item is C; so it is not A.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: shown → chosen → not released. Contrapositive: released → not chosen → not shown. The Long Field was released, so it wasn't chosen, so it wasn't shown. Find the answer that takes an item with the final property and concludes it doesn't have the first one, passing through the middle step.

choices.note: Wrong. Sold → inspected; inspected → not over 100,000 miles. The sedan was inspected (the middle term), so it's under 100,000. That's valid, but it runs forward from the middle, not backward from the end to the start.
Wrong. Member → auditioned; can read music → not turned away. Then concludes Lin is a member because Lin reads music. That's reversed and invalid; not being turned away doesn't make you a member.

Wrong. The closest trap. Gallery → donated by Ames; donated → not pre-1900. The portrait is pre-1900, so Ames didn't donate it. But it stops at the middle term. The original goes all the way to 'not shown,' the first term; C never concludes 'not in the east gallery.'

CORRECT. On menu → prepared by the head chef; prepared by chef → no peanuts. Satay has peanuts, so the chef didn't prepare it, so it's not on the menu. Same chain, same backward run to the first term.
Wrong. Reading room → approved; approved → good condition. Then concludes a book in good condition must be in the reading room. That reverses both conditionals.

questions.stimulus: For decades, groundwater has been pumped heavily for irrigation in the Halden Valley, and as a result the land surface over most of the valley has sunk by more than a meter. In recent years, pumping has continued at the same rate and the water table has kept falling just as fast as before, yet the land has been sinking much more slowly than it did earlier.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: In recent years, rainfall in the Halden Valley has been greater than its long-term average.
Land sinks when the removal of groundwater allows underground layers of fine clay to compact under the weight of the material above them.
Several farms in the valley have recently switched to irrigation methods that use less water.
In a neighboring valley where less groundwater is pumped, the land has sunk by only a few centimeters.
Most of the clay beneath the valley has already compacted almost as far as it can, and the sands that remain barely compact.
questions.explanation: The puzzle is why unchanged pumping and an equally fast-falling water table now produce less sinking. E explains it: the compressible clay has largely finished compacting, and the remaining sands barely compact. B is the tempting trap: it explains why pumping causes sinking at all but not why the sinking has slowed; A and C conflict with the stated facts that the water table and pumping rate are unchanged.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Pumping continues at the same rate and the water table is falling as fast as ever, but the land is now sinking much more slowly.

breakdown.analysis: Same cause, weaker effect. So something about the ground itself must have changed. Prephrase: the stuff that compacts has mostly already compacted. Think of squeezing a sponge: the first squeezes flatten it a lot, but once it's squashed, squeezing just as hard barely changes it.

choices.note: Wrong. Extra rain might slow the water table's fall, but the stimulus says the water table is falling just as fast as before. So rain can't be the explanation.
Wrong. The trap. It explains why pumping makes land sink at all. It doesn't explain why the sinking has slowed while pumping hasn't.
Wrong. Contradicts the facts: pumping has continued at the same rate. Even if some farms use less, the total is unchanged.
Wrong. A comparison with another valley shows that pumping causes sinking, but says nothing about why Halden's sinking slowed down.
CORRECT. The clay that compacts is almost fully compacted, and what's left (sand) barely compresses. So even with the same pumping and water-table drop, there's little left to sink.

questions.stimulus: Dietitian: This year Westbrook Elementary began offering free fruit at lunch, and on average its students now eat fewer cookies and chips at lunch than they did last year. Clearly, offering free fruit leads children to eat fruit in place of snack foods.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the dietitian's argument?
choices: Do Westbrook students prefer some kinds of fruit, such as apples, to other kinds offered at lunch?
Did students at comparable schools without free fruit also eat fewer cookies and chips at lunch this year?
Is fruit generally more nutritious for growing children than cookies and chips are?
How much does it cost Westbrook each year to provide free fruit to students at lunch?
Do Westbrook students eat more cookies and chips at home after school than they did last year?
questions.explanation: The dietitian credits the fruit program for a drop in snack eating, so the key question is whether something else, such as a district-wide change, caused the drop. If comparable schools without free fruit saw the same decline, the program looks irrelevant; if not, the argument is strengthened, so B is useful either way. E is tempting, but the conclusion concerns what children eat at lunch, not at home, and A, C, and D do not bear on the causal claim.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Offering free fruit leads children to eat fruit in place of snack foods.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Westbrook began offering free fruit at lunch this year, and its students now eat fewer cookies and chips at lunch than last year.

breakdown.analysis: Causal claim from a before-and-after change at one school. Maybe something else cut snack eating, like a district snack ban or price hike. The useful question checks for that: did similar schools without fruit see the same drop? If yes, the fruit looks irrelevant. If no, the fruit looks like the cause. Either answer moves the argument, which is what an evaluate answer needs.

choices.note: Wrong. Which fruit they like best doesn't affect whether the fruit program caused the drop in snacks.

CORRECT. A control-group question. If comparable schools without free fruit also saw snack eating drop, something else is the likely cause and the argument weakens. If they didn't, the fruit looks responsible and the argument strengthens.
Wrong. Nutrition is beside the point. The argument is about what kids eat, not whether it's good for them.
Wrong. Cost has nothing to do with whether the fruit caused the change. The LSAT is ultra specific: this is about cause, not cost.
Wrong. Tempting, but the conclusion is about eating fruit in place of snacks at lunch. What kids eat at home after school doesn't test that.

questions.stimulus: Parks official: Critics say that replacing the lawn in Orchard Square with native meadow plants was a mistake because the square now draws fewer visitors. But the meadow has cut the square's water use by 60 percent, and in a survey posted on the square's information board, 85 percent of respondents said they approve of the meadow. So the change has been popular with the public.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the parks official's defense?
choices: Most people who stopped visiting the square after the meadow was planted did so because they preferred the lawn.
The meadow requires more frequent maintenance work by park staff than the old lawn did, which raises the square's labor costs.
Several other cities have replaced lawns in public squares with native plants.
Many of the people who responded to the survey also visit other parks in the city.
Some survey respondents said they would like benches added to the meadow.
questions.explanation: The survey reached only people who still come to the square, so it leaves out exactly those most likely to dislike the change. A confirms that the people who stopped coming did so because they disliked the meadow, so the 85 percent figure does not reflect the public as a whole. B is the tempting trap: it supports the critics' view that the change was a mistake, but it does not touch the official's conclusion that the change is popular.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Replacing the lawn with a native meadow has been popular with the public.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The meadow cut water use by 60 percent; in a survey posted on the square's information board, 85 percent of respondents approved.

breakdown.analysis: Look at who took the survey: people standing in the square reading the board. Those are the people who still come. The people who stopped visiting, the ones most likely to hate the change, never saw it. It's like surveying diners inside a restaurant about whether they like the new menu. The water savings, by the way, are irrelevant to popularity. Prephrase: the survey's sample is biased toward people who like the meadow.

choices.note: CORRECT. This confirms the bias. The people who stopped coming did so because they preferred the lawn, and they're exactly who the board survey missed. So 85 percent approval doesn't speak for the public.
Wrong. The trap. Higher labor costs support the critics' claim that the change was a mistake, but the official's conclusion is about popularity. Cost doesn't touch that.
Wrong. Other cities doing the same thing says nothing about whether Orchard Square's meadow is popular.
Wrong. Respondents visiting other parks doesn't show they misrepresent the public's view of this meadow.
Wrong. Wanting benches added is compatible with approving of the meadow. Doesn't undermine the survey.

questions.stimulus: Film historian: Records show that the silent film The Lantern Keeper was shown in only three cities during its original release, and few reviews of it were published. Yet its distinctive camera techniques appear in dozens of films by directors who began working in the years just after its release. These directors, then, must have seen The Lantern Keeper.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the film historian's argument depends?
choices: Most of the directors who used the techniques lived in or near one of the three cities where the film was shown.
The few published reviews of The Lantern Keeper praised its camera techniques.
The directors who used the techniques were more innovative than most other directors of their time.
The techniques were not described in some widely available publication before those directors began using them.
The Lantern Keeper was seen by more people than the surviving records indicate.
questions.explanation: The historian infers from shared techniques that the directors must have seen the film, which requires ruling out other ways they could have learned the techniques. Negate D: if a widely available publication described the techniques, the directors could have learned them there, and 'must have seen' fails. A and E are attractive because they would make it easier for the directors to have seen the film, but the argument does not need either: a film shown in only three cities could still have reached these directors.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Directors who used the film's camera techniques must have seen The Lantern Keeper.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The film showed in only three cities and got few reviews; its distinctive techniques appear in dozens of films by directors who started soon after its release.

breakdown.analysis: 'Must have seen' is very strong. It assumes there's no other way those directors picked up the techniques. If the techniques were written up somewhere widely read, or passed on by a teacher, the directors needn't have seen the film. Like saying: you know my grandma's secret recipe, so you must have eaten at her house. Not if she published it. Prephrase: the techniques weren't available some other way.

choices.note: Wrong. Not needed. Directors could have traveled to one of those cities, or seen the film later. Negating A doesn't hurt the argument. Tempting because it would make seeing the film easier.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the directors who used the techniques lived in or near one of the three cities.

choices.note: Wrong. What the reviews said isn't required. Even if they ignored the techniques, the directors could have seen the film. Negating B does no damage.
choices.negation: Not all of the few published reviews praised the film's camera techniques.

choices.note: Wrong. Whether these directors were more innovative is irrelevant to whether they saw the film. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: The directors who used the techniques were not more innovative than most other directors of their time.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it and the argument collapses: if a widely available publication described the techniques first, the directors could have learned them by reading, and 'must have seen' fails.
choices.negation: The techniques were described in some widely available publication before those directors began using them.

choices.note: Wrong. It would help, but it isn't required. A film in only three cities could still have reached these directors. Negating E (records are accurate) doesn't break the argument.
choices.negation: The Lantern Keeper was not seen by more people than the surviving records indicate.

questions.stimulus: A utility should postpone shutting off a household's service for nonpayment whenever the household has made at least one partial payment within the past sixty days and, in addition, either someone in the household depends on electrically powered medical equipment or temperatures are forecast to fall below freezing during the following week.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: The Garcias' last partial payment was ninety days ago, but Mr. Garcia relies on a home oxygen machine, so the utility should postpone shutting off their service.
The Whitfields made a partial payment two weeks ago, and no one in the household uses medical equipment; with mild weather forecast, the utility should postpone shutting off their service.
The Lees made a partial payment last month, and a hard freeze is forecast for next week, so the utility should postpone shutting off their service.
The Novaks have made no partial payments this year, although Ms. Novak relies on a powered wheelchair, so the utility is required to shut off their service.
The Ortegas made a partial payment last month and rely on medical equipment, so the utility should not only postpone shutting off their service but also forgive their unpaid balance.
questions.explanation: The principle requires a partial payment within sixty days plus either medical-equipment dependence or a forecast freeze. The Lees meet both parts, so C conforms. D is the subtle trap: the Novaks fail the payment condition, but the principle says only when a shutoff should be postponed, not when one is required; A fails the sixty-day condition, B meets neither of the second conditions, and E adds forgiveness, which the principle never addresses.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: If (partial payment within 60 days) AND (someone depends on powered medical equipment OR a freeze is forecast in the next week) → the utility should postpone shutoff.

breakdown.analysis: Two conditions, and the second is an either/or. You need the payment AND one of medical-equipment-or-freeze. Find a case that meets both and concludes 'postpone.' Note what the principle does NOT say: it never says when a shutoff is required, and never mentions forgiving debt. Failing the condition doesn't trigger the opposite.

choices.note: Wrong. The last partial payment was 90 days ago, so the 60-day condition fails. The oxygen machine alone isn't enough.
Wrong. The payment condition is met, but neither half of the second condition is: no medical equipment and mild weather. The principle doesn't call for postponing.
CORRECT. Partial payment last month (within 60 days) plus a hard freeze forecast for next week. Both parts met, so postpone.

Wrong. The subtle trap. The Novaks do fail the payment condition, but the principle only tells you when to postpone. It never says a shutoff is required otherwise. Failing a sufficient condition doesn't give you the opposite result.
Wrong. The postponement part is fine, but the principle says nothing about forgiving balances. The answer goes beyond the rule.

questions.stimulus: Conservationist: Any bird species in the Pellam Islands whose nests are within reach of the introduced rats is in danger of local extinction unless it breeds more than once a year. Every bird species in danger of local extinction there should be included in the new captive-breeding program. The Pellam rail nests only on the ground, where the rats can reach its nests. So the Pellam rail should be included in the captive-breeding program.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the conservationist's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Only bird species whose nests are within reach of the rats should be included in the captive-breeding program.
The Pellam rail breeds less often than any other bird species in the Pellam Islands.
Any bird species that breeds only once a year is in danger of local extinction if rats can reach its nests.
Every bird species in the Pellam Islands that nests only on the ground breeds more than once a year.
Every bird species in the Pellam Islands that breeds more than once a year nests at least partly off the ground.
questions.explanation: The rail's nests are within the rats' reach, so it is endangered (and belongs in the program) unless it breeds more than once a year; the argument needs to rule that out. By contrapositive, E says that a species nesting only on the ground does not breed more than once a year, which completes the chain. B is the most attractive trap, but breeding less often than every other species is compatible with breeding twice a year; C restates part of the first rule without saying how often the rail breeds, and D would defeat the conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Pellam rail should be included in the captive-breeding program.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nests within rats' reach → endangered, unless the species breeds more than once a year; endangered → should be in the program; the rail nests only on the ground, within the rats' reach.

breakdown.analysis: Translate the 'unless': nests reachable AND NOT breeds more than once a year → endangered → program. The rail's nests are reachable. So the only missing piece is: the rail does not breed more than once a year. Chain: rail → nests only on ground → (need) not breeding more than once a year → endangered → program. Any answer that guarantees a ground-only nester doesn't breed more than once a year closes the gap.

choices.note: Wrong. 'Only' makes this: in program → nests reachable. That's a necessary condition for inclusion, not something that puts the rail in. And it doesn't touch the breeding issue.

Wrong. The trap. Breeding less often than every other species sounds like 'rarely,' but it's a relative claim. If every other species breeds three times a year, the rail could still breed twice, and then it's not endangered by the rule. Watch the switch from a relative claim to an absolute one.
Wrong. This restates part of the first rule but never says how often the rail breeds. Without that, you still can't apply it to the rail.
Wrong. Opposite. If ground-only nesters breed more than once a year, the rail escapes the endangered category, and the conclusion loses its support.

CORRECT. Breeds more than once a year → nests at least partly off the ground. Contrapositive: nests only on the ground → does not breed more than once a year. The rail nests only on the ground, so it breeds once a year or less, so with reachable nests it's endangered, so it belongs in the program.

questions.stimulus: Most of the breakfast cereals sold at Grantham Market are fortified with iron, and most of the iron-fortified cereals sold there are high in sugar. So most of the breakfast cereals sold at Grantham Market are high in sugar.
questions.stem: The pattern of questionable reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: Most of the employees at Dorrit Mills work the night shift, and every night-shift employee there receives a wage premium. So most of the employees at Dorrit Mills receive a wage premium.
Most of the trails in Kessel Forest are open to cyclists, and most of the forest's trails that are open to cyclists are steep. So most of the trails in Kessel Forest are steep.
Most of the novels on Ingrid's shelf are mysteries, and most mysteries are set in cities. So it is likely that at least one novel on Ingrid's shelf is set in a city.
Most of the students in Pell's class passed the exam, and most of those who passed had studied with a tutor. So most of the students who studied with a tutor passed the exam.
Most of the members of the Arden Hiking Club are retired, and the club's president is a member. So the club's president is probably retired.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two 'most' statements, but most of a majority need not be a majority of the whole (60 percent of 60 percent is only 36 percent). B makes the identical error with trails, cyclists, and steepness. A is the strongest trap because it looks the same, but its second premise says 'every,' which makes the conclusion valid; D commits a different error, reversing which group is said to be 'most' of which, while C and E draw modest, reasonable probabilistic conclusions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most cereals sold at Grantham Market are high in sugar.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most cereals there are iron-fortified; most iron-fortified cereals there are high in sugar.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B (among A) are C; so most A are C.

breakdown.analysis: Two 'mosts' don't chain. Most of most can be a minority. Quick numbers: 100 cereals, 60 are fortified, 36 of those (60 percent) are sugary. That's only 36 percent of all cereals. It's like: most of the class went on the trip, and most of the trip-goers got sunburned, so most of the class got sunburned. Not necessarily. Find the answer making that same 'most + most' error.

choices.note: Wrong. The strongest trap because it looks the same. But the second premise says 'every' night-shift employee gets the premium. Most + all does chain: if most work nights and all night workers get the premium, most get the premium. Valid, so not parallel.
CORRECT. Most trails are open to cyclists; most cyclist-open trails are steep; so most trails are steep. Same 'most of most' error. 60 percent of 60 percent is only 36 percent.
Wrong. The conclusion is modest: it's likely at least one novel is set in a city. That's reasonable, not the same overreach. Also, its second premise is about mysteries in general, not on the shelf.
Wrong. A different error: reversal. Most who passed had a tutor doesn't mean most who had a tutor passed. Flawed, but not the same flaw.
Wrong. Most members are retired, so a given member is probably retired. That's a reasonable probabilistic conclusion, not the 'most of most' chain.

questions.stimulus: Granite boulders scattered across the Tamsin Plain are of a type found in place only in the Dovre Mountains, 200 kilometers to the north. Geologists know of only two processes able to carry boulders that far: glaciers and catastrophic floods. Boulders carried by floods are rounded and smoothed, whereas boulders carried by glaciers typically keep sharp edges and often bear parallel scratches. Most of the Dovre granite boulders on the plain have sharp edges, though a few are rounded.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: At least some of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by glaciers.
All of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by a single glacier.
The rounded boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by catastrophic floods.
Most of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain bear parallel scratches.
No catastrophic flood has ever swept from the Dovre Mountains to the Tamsin Plain.
questions.explanation: Flood-carried boulders are rounded, so the many sharp-edged boulders could not have come by flood; since only glaciers and floods could carry them, those boulders were carried by glaciers, as A says. C is the tempting trap: glacier-carried boulders only 'typically' keep sharp edges, so the few rounded ones could also have arrived by glacier. B and E ignore the rounded boulders' uncertain origin, and D overstates 'often bear' scratches.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain come only from the Dovre Mountains, 200 km away; 2) Only glaciers and catastrophic floods can carry boulders that far; 3) Flood-carried boulders are rounded and smoothed; 4) Glacier-carried boulders typically keep sharp edges and often have parallel scratches; 5) Most of the plain's boulders are sharp-edged; a few are rounded.

breakdown.analysis: Use the strict rule, not the loose one. Floods → rounded. Contrapositive: sharp-edged → not carried by flood. Only two options exist, so sharp-edged → glacier. Most boulders are sharp, so at least some (in fact most) came by glacier. The rounded ones are a mystery: glacier boulders only 'typically' stay sharp, so a rounded one could have come either way.

choices.note: CORRECT. Floods always round boulders, so the sharp-edged ones didn't come by flood. With only two possible carriers, they came by glacier. 'At least some' is easily supported.
Wrong. Too strong twice over. The rounded boulders could have come by flood, and nothing says only one glacier was involved.
Wrong. The trap. Floods → rounded doesn't give you rounded → flood. Glacier boulders only 'typically' keep sharp edges, so some rounded ones might have come by glacier too.
Wrong. Glacier boulders 'often' bear scratches, not usually. You can't get to 'most' from 'often.'
Wrong. The rounded boulders may well have come by flood. Nothing rules a flood out.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Two years after the town of Ashby began requiring employers to list salary ranges in job postings, the gap between the average starting salaries of men and women hired by Ashby firms had narrowed considerably. The requirement probably narrowed the gap by giving applicants, many of whom had previously had little idea what a position paid, a firmer basis for negotiating their pay.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?
choices: Since the requirement took effect, far more women than before have applied for positions at Ashby firms of every size.
Some Ashby employers listed salary ranges in their job postings even before the requirement took effect.
Job postings in Ashby that list salary ranges attract more applicants than postings that do not.
The gap narrowed mainly for positions whose starting pay was individually negotiated, and hardly at all for positions with fixed pay scales.
Women hired by Ashby firms since the requirement took effect have, on average, more work experience than women hired before it.
questions.explanation: The economist claims both that the requirement narrowed the gap and that it did so by aiding negotiation. D fits that mechanism precisely: the gap shrank where pay is negotiated and not where pay is fixed, which is hard to explain unless the change worked through negotiation. A is tempting because more female applicants sounds favorable, but a changed applicant pool is an alternative explanation, not support; E likewise offers an alternative cause (more experienced hires), and B, if anything, slightly weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The salary-range requirement probably narrowed the gender gap in starting pay by giving applicants a firmer basis for negotiating.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Two years after Ashby required posted salary ranges, the gap between men's and women's average starting salaries narrowed considerably; many applicants previously had little idea what jobs paid.

breakdown.analysis: Two claims: the requirement caused the narrowing, and it worked through negotiation. The best strengthener supports the mechanism. Think about where negotiation matters: jobs where pay is negotiated, not jobs with fixed scales. If the gap shrank only where people negotiate, that's strong evidence the negotiation story is right. Prephrase: the narrowing happened where negotiation matters.

choices.note: Wrong. Tempting because it sounds pro-women. But a changed applicant pool is a different explanation for the narrowing, not support for the negotiation mechanism. It competes with the economist's story.
Wrong. If some employers already listed ranges, the requirement changed less, which if anything slightly weakens the claim.
Wrong. More applicants doesn't show anything about negotiating pay or the gender gap.

CORRECT. The gap narrowed where pay is negotiated and barely moved where it's fixed. That's exactly the pattern you'd expect if the requirement worked by helping people negotiate, and it's hard to explain otherwise.
Wrong. Alternative cause. More experienced women hires would earn more for that reason, which would explain the narrowing without the requirement.

questions.stimulus: Library board member: Advocates of eliminating overdue fines at Corland's public libraries claim that doing so would increase the number of books borrowed, and they cite a pilot program at the Wexley branch, where borrowing rose after fines were dropped. But the pilot coincided with the opening of a large school next door to the Wexley branch, which by itself could have increased borrowing there. So eliminating overdue fines would not increase the number of books borrowed.
questions.stem: The board member's reasoning is flawed in that the argument
choices: attacks the motives of those who advocate eliminating overdue fines rather than addressing their evidence
relies on a possible explanation of the pilot results without considering whether the new school's students use the library
takes the weakness of the evidence offered for a claim as sufficient grounds for concluding that the claim is false
presumes that an increase in borrowing is the only reason anyone has offered for eliminating overdue fines
assumes that the results of a pilot program at one branch cannot reveal anything about the effects of a citywide policy
questions.explanation: The board member legitimately shows that the Wexley pilot does not establish its conclusion, since the new school is an uncontrolled alternative cause, but then concludes that eliminating fines would not increase borrowing; discrediting the evidence for a claim does not show the claim false, as C says. B is the main trap: offering a possible alternative explanation is enough to undercut the pilot as evidence, so the member need not prove the school's students borrow. D is also tempting, but the argument concerns only borrowing and presumes nothing about other reasons, and E misdescribes the objection, which concerns a confounding event rather than the limits of pilots.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eliminating overdue fines would not increase the number of books borrowed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Advocates cite a Wexley pilot where borrowing rose after fines were dropped; but a large school opened next door at the same time, which alone could have increased borrowing.

breakdown.analysis: The board member does one fair thing and one unfair thing. Fair: pointing out the new school means the pilot doesn't prove fines matter. Unfair: concluding that dropping fines would NOT increase borrowing. Weak evidence for a claim doesn't make the claim false. It's like saying: your only witness was drunk, so you didn't see a UFO. Maybe not, but maybe you did. Prephrase: treats undermined evidence as proof the conclusion is false.

choices.note: Wrong. The member addresses the evidence directly (the pilot and the school). Nothing about motives.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The advocates just don't want to pay their own fines, so their proposal should be ignored.

choices.note: Wrong. The main trap. To undercut evidence, you only need a plausible alternative explanation. The member doesn't have to prove the students use the library. The real problem is the leap at the end, not this step.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Borrowing rose because of the new school, so it wasn't the fines, even though no one checked whether students ever visit the branch.

choices.note: CORRECT. The member shows the pilot evidence is weak, then jumps to 'fines don't matter.' Discrediting the support for a claim doesn't show the claim is false.
Wrong. Tempting, but the argument is only about borrowing and assumes nothing about other reasons for dropping fines.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Dropping fines won't raise borrowing, so there's no reason at all to drop them.

choices.note: Wrong. Misdescribes the objection. The member's complaint is a confounding event at that branch, not that a pilot can never tell you anything about a citywide policy.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The pilot was at just one branch, so it can tell us nothing about what would happen across the city.
